title: Speeding up and slowing down a change: warmth, stirring, powder, crowds and helpers

summary.text: A sachet of fruit salt fizzes for about half a minute in a glass of water. In a glass of fridge-cold water, the same powder takes much longer. The powder and the water are the same, so what changed? Your child times the fizz in cold, room-temperature and warm water, then speeds up and slows down the browning of an apple. They find that every way of speeding up a change works by making particles meet more often or more strongly. They also meet catalysts, helpers that are not used up, from enzymes in food to the metal in a car's exhaust. They hear how a Scottish chemist, Elizabeth Fulhame, found a helper hiding in plain water in 1794. Then they ask why the Delhi Iron Pillar has stood for about 1,600 years.
summary.art: Three glasses in a row on a kitchen counter, cold, room-temperature and warm, with a different amount of fizz in each and a clock beside each glass.

intro.hook: Open one sachet of fruit salt. Drop half a teaspoon into cold water from the fridge, and the same amount into warm water. The warm glass finishes fizzing long before the cold one. Why does warmth make the same powder hurry?
intro.text: The powder never changes. The water never changes. Only the warmth does, and the change speeds up. Reactions are changes that make new substances, and you met fast and slow ones in Class 3. Now you find out how to steer the speed. You will time the fizz, race browning apples, and test what stirring, crowding and powder do. Then you meet helpers called catalysts, which speed up a change and come out unchanged.
intro.art: A hand holding a sachet of fruit salt over two glasses, one with a few lazy bubbles and one with a busy stream of bubbles.

outcomes: I can explain that a reaction happens when particles of different substances meet, and that its speed is how much new substance forms in each second.
I can name four ways to speed up a reaction (warmth, stirring, smaller pieces and more crowding) and explain each one as more or harder meetings of particles.
I can run a fair test with cups at three temperatures, time each one, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that a catalyst speeds up one kind of reaction and is not used up, and name catalysts in food, in cars and in my body.
I can explain how cold, a barrier, lime juice or a coating slows a change, and why too much heat stops an enzyme.
I can read a graph of a reaction over time and explain why it starts fast and then slows.
I can tell how Elizabeth Fulhame and the Delhi Iron Pillar show that a change depends on what can touch what.

terms.meaning: How fast a reaction goes. It is how much new substance forms in each second, minute or year.
terms.example: Fruit salt in warm water makes its bubbles in about 15 seconds. In cold water the same bubbles take much longer, so the rate is lower.
terms.art: A stopwatch beside a glass of fizzing water with a few bubbles counted.

terms.meaning: A substance that goes into a reaction and is used up as it changes.
terms.example: In fruit salt, the baking soda and the citric acid are the reactants. They meet in water and are used up.
terms.art: Two arrows pointing from a spoon of baking soda and a lemon into one glass.

terms.meaning: A new substance that a reaction makes.
terms.example: The bubbles in a fizzing glass are carbon dioxide gas, a product of baking soda meeting citric acid.
terms.art: An arrow leaving a glass with bubbles rising out of it.

terms.meaning: The tiny bits that every substance is made of. They are far too small to see, and they are always moving.
terms.example: In warm water the particles move faster than in cold water, so a warm cup of tea cools as they slow down.
terms.art: Round dots of two colours moving in a glass, with small motion lines behind each dot.

terms.meaning: A bump between two particles. A reaction can only happen when particles collide.
terms.example: Billions of water particles bump into a sugar lump every second, and a few bumps are enough to pull sugar particles off it.
terms.art: Two dots meeting in the middle of the picture with a small starburst between them.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold something is. It tells us how fast its particles are moving.
terms.example: A thermometer in warm water reads about 50 degrees. In fridge water it reads about 5 degrees.
terms.art: A thermometer standing in a glass of water with a scale from 0 to 100.

terms.meaning: The size of the outside of a thing, where it can touch whatever is around it. Cutting a thing into small pieces gives it more surface area.
terms.example: A grated apple has far more surface area than the same apple in one piece, so more of it touches the air.
terms.art: A whole cube beside the same cube cut into eight small cubes, with the outsides coloured.

terms.meaning: How crowded the particles of a substance are in a space. Many particles in a small space means a high concentration.
terms.example: Lime juice squeezed into two spoons of water is more concentrated than the same juice in twelve spoons of water.
terms.art: Two glasses of the same size, one with many dots and one with few.

terms.meaning: Moving a liquid so that its particles mix and meet new neighbours.
terms.example: A spoon in a cup of tea carries sugar particles away from the lump and brings in fresh water.
terms.art: A spoon making a swirl in a glass of cloudy water.

terms.meaning: A substance that makes one kind of reaction go faster and is not used up. It comes out of the reaction the same as it went in.
terms.example: The metal inside a car's exhaust pipe helps poisonous gas turn into safer gas, and the metal stays in the pipe for years.
terms.art: A small helper dot sitting between two reactant dots, with an arrow showing the same helper dot afterwards.

terms.meaning: A catalyst made by a living being. Each enzyme helps only one job.
terms.example: Catalase in a potato breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. An enzyme in an apple turns a cut surface brown.
terms.art: A big folded enzyme shape with a small particle fitting into a hollow in it.

terms.meaning: Something that slows the changes that spoil food.
terms.example: Salt, oil, chilli and lime in a mango pickle slow down the changes that would make the mangoes rot.
terms.art: A jar of mango pickle with salt, oil and chilli drawn beside it.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
terms.example: To test warmth, you use the same amount of fruit salt and the same amount of water in every cup.
terms.art: Three identical cups in a row with only the temperature label different.

terms.meaning: The cup or sample where you change nothing, so you can compare the others with it.
terms.example: In the apple test, the plain chunk left on a plate is the control. You compare the lime chunk with it.
terms.art: Four plates of apple, one marked as the control with a star.

terms.meaning: The orange-brown flaky substance that forms when iron slowly reacts with oxygen and water.
terms.example: A balcony grill in Chennai, near the sea, rusts faster than one in a dry town.
terms.art: An iron nail half covered with orange-brown rust, beside a bright new nail.

explanations.concept: A reaction is a meeting of particles
explanations.definition: A chemical reaction happens when particles of different substances meet and rearrange into new substances.
explanations.description: Dry fruit salt can sit in a sachet for months. Its two powders, baking soda and citric acid, are side by side but locked in dry grains. Add water, and the powders dissolve. Their particles are now free to move and meet. When a baking soda particle meets a citric acid particle in the right way, they rearrange into new particles. One of the new substances is carbon dioxide gas, and that is the fizz. So a reaction is something that happens between substances, not inside one of them. If the particles never meet, nothing happens. This is why 'how fast' always means 'how often and how well do the particles meet?'
examples: Dry fruit salt in a sachet does nothing. In water, it fizzes within seconds.
A steel grill in a dry cupboard rusts very slowly. In a wet balcony it rusts faster, because water and oxygen reach the iron.
Dry baking soda and dry lime powder can sit together in a jar. Add a few drops of water and they fizz.
explanations.art: Dry grains of two colours sitting still, then dissolved in water with dots of both colours moving and meeting, and a bubble forming.

explanations.concept: Reaction rate: how fast a change goes
explanations.definition: The rate of a reaction is how much new substance it makes, or how much old substance it uses up, in a given time.
explanations.description: Chemists measure rate with a clock. They might time how long bubbles last, how much gas fills a balloon in a minute, or how quickly a colour fades. A reaction that makes a lot of product in a short time has a high rate. A reaction that takes a year to make a little rust has a low rate. Rates cover an enormous range. A spark in a cracker finishes in a thousandth of a second. A diamond turning into graphite is so slow that nobody has ever seen it happen. The same ideas work all the way along this range.
examples: Fruit salt in warm water: a high rate, over in about 15 seconds.
An iron gate rusting: a low rate, visible only after months.
A banana skin spotting: a middle rate, over a few days.
explanations.art: A long line from 'a cracker bang' on the left to 'diamond becoming graphite' on the right, with a kitchen fizz and a rusting gate placed along it.

explanations.concept: A reaction starts fast and then slows down
explanations.definition: In most reactions, the rate is highest at the start and falls steadily as the reactants get used up.
explanations.description: Watch a glass of fruit salt. At first, the bubbles race up, because there are many fresh particles of both powders to meet. After some seconds, many have already reacted. There are fewer particles left to meet, so fewer bubbles rise each second. In the end, one of the reactants runs out and the fizz stops. If you draw the amount of product against time, you get a curve. It climbs steeply at the start, then bends over and flattens. A flat curve does not mean the reaction is boring. It means one of the reactants is used up.
examples: The bubbles in a glass of fruit salt are fiercest in the first few seconds.
A tea bag colours the water fast at first, and then more slowly.
A burning agarbatti burns steadily, but a heap of crackers is done in a flash because everything is lit at once.
explanations.art: A graph with seconds along the bottom and amount of gas up the side, with a curve that rises steeply and then flattens, and three glasses drawn under the start, the middle and the end.

explanations.concept: Warmth speeds up almost every reaction
explanations.definition: Raising the temperature makes particles move faster, so they meet more often and more forcefully, and the reaction goes faster.
explanations.description: Temperature is a measure of how fast the particles in a thing are moving. In warm water they zoom around faster than in cold water. Faster particles bump into each other more often. They also bump harder, and a hard bump is more likely to rearrange them into something new. For many reactions near room temperature, a rise of about 10 degrees roughly doubles the rate. That is a rule of thumb, not an exact law. It is why milk goes off faster on a hot day, why a pressure cooker cooks dal quickly, and why a fridge keeps food fresh longer. Warmth is not magic. It just means more meetings, and stronger ones. Dissolving sugar is not a reaction, because no new substance forms, but the same idea of meetings helps explain why hot tea dissolves it faster.
examples: A pressure cooker raises the cooking temperature above that of an open pot, so dal cooks in a fraction of the time.
Milk turns sour much faster on a hot afternoon than in the fridge.
Sugar dissolves faster in hot tea than in cold water.
explanations.art: Two glasses of water with the same dots, short arrows on the dots in the cold glass and long arrows on the dots in the warm glass, with more bumps marked in the warm one.

explanations.concept: Stirring and moving: bringing fresh particles together
explanations.definition: Stirring makes a reaction faster because it keeps carrying used-up particles away and bringing fresh ones to meet.
explanations.description: In a still glass, the particles at the bottom of a lump of fruit salt meet only the water that happens to be next to them. After they react, that nearby water is full of the new substance, and new water is slow to arrive. A spoon swirls the water around, so fresh water keeps reaching the powder. Stirring does not make particles move faster. It brings new partners to the meeting. That is a different way to get the same result as warmth, which is more meetings per second.
examples: Stirring the sugar in a tumbler of tea dissolves it faster.
Swirling a dal pot stops the bottom from burning, because fresh dal keeps moving to the hot floor of the pot.
A washing machine keeps tossing clothes so that fresh detergent water reaches the dirt.
explanations.art: A spoon swirling in one glass with arrows bringing in fresh water to a lump, and another still glass with a ring of used-up water sitting around the lump.

explanations.concept: Smaller pieces mean more surface and faster reactions
explanations.definition: A solid can only react where it touches the other substance. Cutting it into small pieces gives it more surface area, so it reacts faster.
explanations.description: A cube with sides of 2 centimetres has six faces, each 4 square centimetres, so its surface area is 24 square centimetres. Cut it into eight small cubes with sides of 1 centimetre, and each has a surface area of 6 square centimetres. Altogether they have 48 square centimetres, double the surface, from the same amount of stuff. More of the solid can now touch the air or the liquid. That is why grated apple browns faster than a chunk, why powdered medicine dissolves faster than a pill, and why a heap of fine flour dust in a mill can explode when a lump of flour cannot. Flour dust has so much surface area that the whole cloud of it burns at once.
examples: Grated apple browns in minutes. A whole apple takes hours.
A lump of jaggery dissolves slowly in water. Powdered jaggery dissolves fast.
Flour mills and grain stores have a risk of dust explosions, because fine dust burns almost instantly in the air.
explanations.art: One large cube with its faces coloured, and next to it the same cube cut into eight small cubes with every new face coloured too, showing the doubled surface.

explanations.concept: Crowding: more particles in the same space
explanations.definition: A higher concentration means more particles in each bit of space, so they meet more often and the reaction goes faster.
explanations.description: Imagine a hall with six people walking about. They hardly ever bump into each other. Now put sixty people into the same hall. They bump all the time. It is the same with particles. Lime juice in two spoons of water has many acid particles near each baking soda particle. Lime juice in twelve spoons of water has the same acid particles spread out, so meetings are rarer. Concentration also works for gases. In pure oxygen, a glowing splint bursts into flame, because oxygen particles are five times more crowded than in air, where only about one particle in five is oxygen. This is why hospitals keep flames far from oxygen cylinders.
examples: Strong vinegar on baking soda fizzes harder than weak vinegar.
A glowing splinter bursts into flame in pure oxygen, but only glows in air.

Deep inside the Sun, hydrogen particles are squashed so tightly that they sometimes join. Even there, an average particle waits billions of years for its turn. This is a different kind of change, but speed still depends on how often particles meet.
explanations.art: Two identical boxes, one with a few dots spread far apart and one with many dots packed close, with more bump stars marked in the packed box.

explanations.concept: A catalyst makes one reaction faster and is not used up
explanations.definition: A catalyst is a substance that lowers the effort a reaction needs, so it goes faster, and the catalyst comes out unchanged.
explanations.description: Think of a mountain pass. Walkers can climb over the high mountain, which is hard and slow. A catalyst is like a lower pass cut through the same mountain. Many more walkers get across in the same time, and the pass is still there afterwards. In a reaction, the particles need a good bump, and in some cases a lot of energy to start changing. A catalyst gives them an easier path. It does not change which substances you start with or which ones you end up with, and it does not change how much product you finally get. It only changes how fast. Most catalysts also help only one kind of reaction, like a key made for one lock.
examples: The potato's catalase makes hydrogen peroxide break down in seconds instead of months.
In a car's exhaust, a honeycomb coated with the metals platinum, palladium and rhodium changes poisonous carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide. The metals are not used up.

Iron helps in factories to join nitrogen from the air with hydrogen to make ammonia for fertiliser. Somewhere between four and five in every ten people alive eat food grown with fertiliser made this way.
explanations.art: A mountain with a high path labelled 'no catalyst' and a low tunnel labelled 'with catalyst', and the same walker figures coming out of both ends.

explanations.concept: Enzymes: living catalysts that work at body warmth
explanations.definition: An enzyme is a catalyst made by a living being. Each enzyme speeds up one job, and most work best in a narrow range of warmth.
explanations.description: Your body cannot cook its food at a high temperature. It must break down food at about 37 degrees. Enzymes make that possible. One enzyme can speed up a reaction by a huge amount. A famous one, studied by Richard Wolfenden and his team, turns a job that would take about 78 million years into a fraction of a second. Because enzymes are folded chains with a special shape, heat can ruin them. A hot dip of just-boiled water ruins the enzyme that turns apple brown. That is why dipped apple stays pale. So heat speeds up reactions but also breaks enzymes, and living beings keep their warmth in a narrow, safe range.
examples: An enzyme in a cut apple helps oxygen turn some of the apple's own chemicals brown.
Saliva has an enzyme that begins to break down starch in rice.
Many washing powders contain enzymes that break down stains of food and sweat. Check the label.
explanations.art: A big folded enzyme shape holding a food particle in a hollow, then releasing two smaller particles, with a flame icon showing the enzyme coming apart in heat.

explanations.concept: Slowing a change down on purpose
explanations.definition: To slow a reaction, do the opposite of speeding it up: cool it, keep the reactants apart, make them less crowded, or block the helper.
explanations.description: People have been slowing reactions for thousands of years, long before they knew why. A fridge cools food, so changes that spoil it go slowly. A sealed jar keeps out oxygen. Salt, oil and chilli in pickle make it hard for spoiling microbes to live. A coat of paint on an iron gate keeps water and oxygen away from the iron. Lime juice on cut apple is acidic and slows the enzyme that turns it brown. In each case, the aim is the same: fewer, weaker meetings. Some medicines are coated so that they dissolve slowly in the stomach and work for hours.
examples: Cut apple dipped in lime juice stays pale for much longer than plain cut apple.
A painted iron gate lasts for years, but a bare one is quickly covered in rust.
Hydrogen peroxide is sold in brown bottles, because light speeds up its breakdown.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: a fridge, a sealed jar, a painted gate and a pickle jar, each with a slow-down arrow.

explanations.concept: Some changes are so slow that we never see them
explanations.definition: Every reaction has a rate, but some rates are so low that nothing visible happens in a human lifetime.
explanations.description: Diamond is made only of carbon. Graphite, the black stuff in a pencil, is also only carbon. At normal air pressure, graphite is the steadier form. So diamond is always very slowly turning into graphite. But the rate is so low that a diamond ring will not change in a million lifetimes. Slow does not mean stopped. It means rare meetings and a very hard job for each one. The Delhi Iron Pillar shows another way to slow things down. Iron really does keep trying to rust. But a thin skin on the pillar keeps most of the water and air away from the iron below, so the rate is very low.
examples: Diamond turning into graphite is too slow to see.
The Delhi Iron Pillar has rusted only a little in about 1,600 years.
Old paper turns yellow over decades.
explanations.art: A diamond ring on the left and a pencil lead on the right, with a very long thin arrow between them marked 'longer than a lifetime'.

explanations.concept: Not every bump makes a reaction
explanations.definition: Most bumps between particles change nothing. A reaction needs the particles to bump hard enough, and in the right way.
explanations.description: At room temperature, one particle in the air bumps into others billions of times in a second. If every bump led to a reaction, everything around us would change in a flash. Most bumps are like two people brushing shoulders in a crowd. Only a rare bump has enough energy, hitting the right way round, to break old links and make new ones. Scientists call the energy needed the activation energy. You can picture it as a hill that particles must get over. Warmth gives more particles enough speed to get over the hill. A catalyst lowers the hill. You will study this picture in more detail in Class 5.
examples: A bump between two baking soda and citric acid particles sometimes does nothing.
Heating a gas makes more of its particles fast enough to get over the hill.
An enzyme lowers the hill, so many more bumps work at body warmth.
explanations.art: Two dots bumping and bouncing apart with an arrow saying 'no change', and another pair bumping hard, flashing and turning into new shapes, with a small hill drawn under the path.

agreed.text: A reaction needs its particles to meet, and anything that makes meetings more frequent or more forceful speeds it up.
agreed.evidence: Warm water, stirring, powder and a higher concentration each speed up a reaction in the lab and in the kitchen. The particle picture explains all four.

agreed.text: For many reactions near room temperature, a rise of about 10 degrees roughly doubles the rate.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of many reactions show this pattern, but not all, and the exact number differs. It is a rule of thumb, first noticed by Jacobus van 't Hoff in the 1880s.

agreed.text: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, and does not change the final amount of product.
agreed.evidence: The same potato or the same metal can be used again and again. Chemists weigh a catalyst before and after and find the same mass.

agreed.text: Enzymes are catalysts made by living beings, and heat above a certain point destroys them.
agreed.evidence: A fruit dipped in just-boiled water stops browning, because the enzyme has been ruined. Raw potato makes peroxide foam, but boiled potato hardly does.

agreed.text: Slow reactions do not stop. They only happen so rarely that we cannot see the change.
agreed.evidence: Very sensitive instruments can detect the slow rusting of an iron pillar and the slow breakdown of old paper.

agreed.text: A thin skin that sticks tightly to a metal can slow its rusting a great deal.
agreed.evidence: Scientists at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur found a thin protective skin on the Delhi Iron Pillar, and showed that it shields the iron below.

challenging.claim: A catalyst can make a reaction happen that would never happen on its own.
challenging.for: A catalyst can turn a change that takes millions of years into one that takes a second, so it can look like magic.
challenging.against: A catalyst only speeds up a reaction that was already possible. It does not change the products or the final amount. Peroxide breaks down on its own, just very slowly.

challenging.claim: If you heat something more, it always reacts faster.
challenging.who: Many people, and some old cookery advice.
challenging.for: For most simple reactions, the rate does rise with temperature, as in the fruit salt test.
challenging.against: Enzymes fall apart in too much heat, so heat can stop the reaction. A dipped apple does not brown because the heat ruined its enzyme. A pan of milk heated too hard catches and burns instead of cooking.

challenging.claim: Old window glass has flowed downwards over the centuries, which is why it is thicker at the bottom.
challenging.who: A popular story, repeated in many books.
challenging.for: Many old panes really are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.against: Calculations by Edgar Zanotto in 1998 showed that glass at room temperature would need far longer than the age of the universe to flow that much. Old window panes were made by spinning molten glass into a disc, which made them uneven from the start. Workers often fitted the heavy edge at the bottom.

challenging.claim: Salty air makes iron rust faster.
challenging.who: Painters and engineers in coastal cities such as Chennai, Kochi and Mumbai.
challenging.for: Railings and grills near the sea need painting more often. Salt dissolved in a film of water helps electric charge move, which speeds the rusting.
challenging.against: Very few scientists disagree. The size of the effect depends on wind, wet weather and the kind of iron.

challenging.claim: Cold stops microbes and chemical changes in food completely.
challenging.who: Some people who leave food in the fridge for weeks.
challenging.for: A fridge keeps milk fresh for days longer than a shelf does.
challenging.against: A fridge only slows the changes. Even in a freezer, some reactions go on very slowly, which is why frozen food still has a limit.

big_questions.q: A grown mayfly may live for only a day, and an iron pillar stands for 1,600 years. To the mayfly, the pillar never changes at all. Is 'slow' a property of the change, or of the one who is watching it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what 'slow' would mean to a mayfly, to you, and to a mountain.

big_questions.q: Are we seeing the same change differently, or are we seeing different changes? A rusting nail, a flame and the Sun are all particles meeting, but they look nothing alike.
big_questions.hint: Think about how slow, fast and hot hide the fact that they are the same kind of change.

big_questions.q: Which changes in your life do you want to speed up, and which do you want to slow down? Who decides?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, learning, healing and friendships.

big_questions.q: Your body runs thousands of reactions at 37 degrees, each at just the right speed. What is keeping them in balance, since no one is in charge?
big_questions.hint: Think about enzymes, and about what happens when you have a fever.

big_questions.q: A catalyst takes part in a change and comes out exactly the same. Does it count as part of the change, or only a bystander?
big_questions.hint: Think about the potato in the peroxide, and the walker's low pass in the mountain.

big_questions.q: If nothing in the universe is ever really still, only slow, what does it mean to call something 'stable'?
big_questions.hint: Think about diamonds, iron and glass.

big_questions.q: Some of the fastest changes, like a flame, and some of the slowest, like a rusting pillar, are the same kind of event. What does that tell you about how you divide the world into 'fast' and 'slow'?
big_questions.hint: Think about how scientists measure both with the same idea.

big_questions.q: Many things that keep us alive, like digestion, depend on slowing a change down just enough. What would a world with only fast changes be like, and what would a world with only slow changes be like?
big_questions.hint: Think of a world where food burned like a firework, and a world where it never changed.

story.title: Sixteen Hundred Summers
story.note: A made-up story around a real place. The Iron Pillar stands in the Qutb complex in Mehrauli, Delhi. It is about 1,600 years old, and it has rusted very little. Scientists at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur found a thin, tightly stuck protective skin on it. Gayathri, Thatha, Rashmi Madam and the talk between them are imagined.
text: In May, the heat in Delhi pressed down like a hand. Gayathri was in Class 4, and she had come from Coimbatore with her grandfather, Thatha. The thermometer on the bus said forty-one degrees.

Thatha had spent forty years as an engineer on the railways. He walked slowly now, with a cap on his head and a cloth over his neck. He stopped talking at once when they came round a corner in the Qutb complex and saw the pillar.
It stood alone in a courtyard. It was a dark, smooth column of iron, taller than three grown men standing on each other's shoulders. A low fence kept visitors back.
'Sixteen hundred years old,' said the guide, a young woman called Rashmi Madam, with a cloth bag on her shoulder. 'Older than the fort. Older than the tower beside it.'
Thatha said nothing for a long time. Then he said, very quietly, 'It is impossible.'
'Why?' asked Gayathri.

'Iron rusts, Gayathri. I spent forty years painting iron bridges so they would not fall into the river. Every five years, new paint. Each time, I scraped off rust as thick as a biscuit. Iron wants to rust. It always has. And this one has stood in the sun and the monsoon for sixteen hundred summers.' He shook his head. 'It must be special iron that does not want to rust.'

Gayathri was thinking about her nails. Before the trip, she had put five iron nails in five jars on the balcony. One had dry air. One had plain water. One had salty water. One had oil. One had vinegar. In three days the salty nail was covered with orange flakes, and the bottom of the jar had a heap of orange powder. The dry nail had only a thin dark skin. The nail in oil was still bright.
'Thatha,' she said slowly, 'my salty nail made a lot of rust. But the rust did not stay on. It fell off in flakes. And then the nail was bare again, and it rusted some more.'
'Yes,' said Thatha. 'Flaking rust is the engineer's enemy. It peels, and fresh iron is open to the damp again.'

'But the dry nail had a thin dark skin, and the skin stayed stuck,' said Gayathri. 'That nail did not rust any more. So maybe the iron is the same, Thatha. Maybe the pillar is not special iron. Maybe it has a skin that does not peel.'
Thatha turned and looked at her as if she had said something in a new language.

Rashmi Madam smiled. 'May I tell you what the scientists found?' she said. 'They looked at the pillar's surface with strong instruments. They found a very thin skin, thinner than a sheet of paper, made of iron joined with oxygen, hydrogen and phosphorus. It sticks tightly. The iron of the pillar also has a lot of phosphorus in it, more than the iron on your bridges. The skin has slowly built up over many years. It keeps most of the water and air from touching the iron below.'
'So the iron still wants to rust,' said Thatha.
'It still tries,' said Rashmi Madam. 'But it hardly ever gets the chance. Every year, a tiny bit more rust forms, so the pillar is not perfect. It is just very, very slow.'
Gayathri looked at the fence. 'Did people touch it a lot?'

'Oh yes. For a long time, visitors stood with their backs to it and tried to reach their arms around it. They said a wish would come true. That hand-oil and sweat wore on the skin. That is why the fence is here now.'
'It is hot today,' Gayathri said. 'Heat speeds up almost everything. At forty-one degrees, why is the pillar still slow?'
'Because the skin is winning,' said Rashmi Madam. 'Heat helps the iron and the air meet. The skin keeps them apart. And the skin is stronger than the heat.'

Thatha took off his cap and stared at the pillar in the sun. He had known for forty years that rust was a slow fire. But he had thought of it as a thing about the iron, a stubborn fact like a river flowing downhill. He had never thought of it as a meeting that could be stopped from happening.
'Forty years of paint,' he said, 'and a girl in Class 4 tells me the iron was never the problem. It was the meeting.'
'You did the same thing,' said Gayathri. 'Paint is a skin too. It keeps iron and water apart.'
Thatha laughed so loudly that a family nearby turned round. 'My bridges would have lasted longer,' he said, 'if I had known to ask for that.'

That evening on the train, Gayathri drew the pillar in her notebook. She drew the iron inside it, and she drew the thin skin round it. She drew water and air outside the skin, with little arrows that could not get through.
Under the drawing she wrote one line. 'Slow does not mean the iron does not try. It means the iron hardly ever gets to meet the air.'
Thatha read it twice, and then tucked the notebook gently into his shirt pocket, as though it were a ticket.
story.epiphany: The pillar is slow because of what stands between the iron and the air. The iron itself is not special.
ask: Gayathri and Thatha explained the pillar in different ways. Which explanation do you find more convincing, and why?
Paint, oil and a stuck-on skin all slow rusting. What do they have in common?
How could you test whether the skin, and not the iron, is why the pillar rusts so slowly?
art: A girl and an older man in a cap standing in a courtyard in front of a tall dark iron pillar behind a low fence, under a hot white sky.
A balcony shelf with five jars, each holding an iron nail, one in dry air, one in plain water, one in salty water, one in oil and one in vinegar.
A cross-section drawing of the iron pillar with a very thin skin around it, and little arrows of air and water stopped outside the skin.
A girl writing in a notebook on a train seat, with her grandfather reading over her shoulder.

roots.context: You timed fizzing cups, raced apples and met helpers called catalysts. Now we ask what the speed of a change tells us about how things happen at all.

deep_truth.truth: A change is not something one substance does alone. It happens when things meet. Warmth, stirring, crowding and powder do not push a change. They only make meetings more often or harder, so slowing a change means keeping things apart.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'Eno fizzes' or 'iron rusts' as if the change lived inside one substance, like its colour. But dry Eno does not fizz, and a painted gate does not rust. The change belongs to the meeting.
deep_truth.evidence: Dry fruit salt sat still. In water, it fizzed, and it fizzed faster in warm water, stirred water and a more crowded mix. The Delhi Iron Pillar has the same iron as a rusting gate, but a tight skin keeps it from meeting water and air.

three.who_am_i: Your body runs thousands of reactions every second at 37 degrees, each at the right speed. You are a set of meetings, kept in balance.
three.what_is_life: A living being is a place where particles meet at just the right speed. Enzymes make the useful meetings happen fast, and warmth, food and water keep them going.
three.what_is_this_world: From a lit match to a rusting pillar to a slowly shining star, everything changes through meetings. Fast and slow are what we call the meetings, depending on how long we can watch.

roots.thread: Fruit salt, a pickle jar, an apple and an iron pillar seem to have nothing in common. In each, particles meet and change into something new, and the speed depends on how often and how hard they meet. A flame and a rusting gate are the same kind of change, at very different speeds. Nothing is ever fully still. Things we call stable are only changing very slowly. The world is a vast number of meetings, some quick and some slow, all part of one whole.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, as reported by Plato in Cratylus 402a
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker, is said to have taught that everything flows, and that you cannot step into the same river twice. The water keeps moving, so the river is never the same.
teachings.link: A rusting nail, a ripening banana and a fizzing glass are all flowing in a way. They look still, but their particles are always meeting and changing.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha is recorded as teaching that all made things are impermanent. Nothing made of parts stays the same.
teachings.link: The Delhi Iron Pillar looks as if it will last forever. But a very slow reaction is working on it all the time. Slow is not the same as still.

teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna, a Buddhist teacher in India about 1,800 years ago, argued that nothing happens by itself. Every event depends on causes and conditions meeting.
teachings.link: Fizz needs dry powders, water and the right warmth to meet. Take away one, and nothing happens.

science.text: Temperature measures how fast the particles in a thing are moving. Reactions slow in the cold, but they do not stop, even in the deepest freezer.

Some scientists think that in certain enzymes, tiny hydrogen particles can pass through the energy hill instead of climbing over it, a quantum effect called tunnelling. How much this speeds up enzymes is still argued.

other_view.who: Parmenides, a Greek philosopher from about 500 BCE
other_view.view: Parmenides argued that change is an illusion. What truly exists simply is, and never comes to be or passes away. He thought that our senses fool us when we think things change.

practice.title: Feel a slow burning
practice.say: Rub your hands together for five seconds. Now hold one palm against your cheek and breathe slowly. The warmth you feel is partly slow burning, as your cells use oxygen to release energy from food. It is happening in every cell now, with the help of enzymes. Breathe in three times and notice the warmth.
practice.kid: Rub your palms for five seconds. Press one to your cheek. Feel the warmth. Your cells are slowly burning food right now. Breathe in three times.

ask: If dry Eno never fizzes, is the fizz in the powder, in the water, or in the meeting?
If a thing only looks still because its change is slow, what else around you might be changing too slowly to see?
Is the pillar's skin part of the pillar, or part of the air around it?
roots.art: An iron nail, a fizzing glass and a lit match drawn in a row, each with small arrows between particles showing the same kind of meeting at three different speeds.

games.title: Which Speed-Up? A card game
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card describes something in daily life. You decide whether it is warmth, stirring, smaller pieces, a crowd, a helper or a slow-down.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with six word tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while two others each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else puts a token face down.

setup.art: Tokens turned over together and the reader showing the answer on the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: an everyday situation on the front, and the speed-up with the reason on the back

items.f: Sugar dissolves much faster in hot tea than in cold water.
items.b: Warmth. Hot water has faster particles, so they meet the sugar more often and harder.

items.f: Amma stirs sugar into milk with a spoon, and it vanishes sooner.
items.b: Stirring. The spoon brings fresh milk to the sugar and carries used-up milk away.

items.f: Powdered jaggery dissolves in water faster than a big lump.
items.b: Smaller pieces. Powder has far more surface touching the water.

items.f: Strong vinegar on baking soda fizzes harder than the same vinegar mixed with lots of water.
items.b: More crowded. More acid particles in the same space meet the baking soda more often.

items.f: Raw potato makes hydrogen peroxide foam within seconds, and the potato is still there afterwards.
items.b: A helper. Potato holds catalase, a catalyst, which is not used up.

items.f: A pressure cooker cooks dal in a fraction of the time of an open pot.
items.b: Warmth. Trapped steam raises the water above 100 degrees, so cooking is faster.

items.f: Potato cubes cook faster than a whole potato of the same weight.
items.b: Smaller pieces. Cubes have more surface, so heat and water enter faster.

items.f: A bottle of milk in the fridge stays fresh for days longer than one on the shelf.
items.b: Slowing down. Cold means slower particles, so the changes that spoil milk go slowly.

items.f: A painted iron gate stays bright for years, but a bare one rusts quickly.
items.b: Slowing down. Paint keeps water and oxygen away from the iron.

items.f: Lime juice on cut apple keeps it pale for hours.
items.b: Slowing down. The acid makes the browning enzyme work poorly.

items.f: A flour mill worker worries about the fine dust in the air.
items.b: Smaller pieces. Fine dust has so much surface that it can burn almost all at once.

items.f: The metal in a car's exhaust changes harmful gas into safer gas, and lasts for years.
items.b: A helper. A catalytic converter is a catalyst, so the metal is not used up.

items.f: A washing powder with enzymes lifts food stains in cool water.
items.b: A helper. Enzymes are catalysts made by living beings, and they speed up the breakdown of the stain.

items.f: A glowing splint bursts into flame in pure oxygen.
items.b: More crowded. Pure oxygen has about five times more oxygen particles in each space than air does.

items.f: A dosa cooks faster on a hotter tawa.
items.b: Warmth. A hotter tawa gives more particles enough energy to react.

items.f: Swirling a glass of fruit salt makes the fizz stop sooner.
items.b: Stirring. Swirling brings fresh water to the powder.

items.f: Hydrogen peroxide is sold in a dark brown bottle.
items.b: Slowing down. Light speeds up its breakdown, and the dark bottle keeps light out.

items.f: Crushed garlic and ginger flavour a curry faster than whole pieces.
items.b: Smaller pieces. Crushing opens more surface, so the flavour comes out quicker.

items.f: A fertiliser factory passes nitrogen and hydrogen over hot iron to make ammonia.
items.b: A helper. The iron is a catalyst that helps the very strong nitrogen particles react.

items.f: Mango pickle is packed with salt, oil and chilli.
items.b: Slowing down. They make it hard for the changes and the microbes that spoil mangoes to carry on.

printables.title: 12 speed-up tokens: two sets of six

rules: Cut out the 20 cards and the 12 tokens. Each player needs one set of the six tokens, so copy the words onto paper if you have too few.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. The six tokens are Warmth, Stirring, Smaller pieces, More crowded, A helper, and Slowing down.
Everyone turns their token over together. The reader turns the card around and reads the back aloud.
A player whose token matches the first words of the back scores one point.
The reader's job passes to the player on the left after each card. With two players, swap after each card.
To play alone, read each front, guess the speed-up in your head and then check the back. Your score is how many you got right out of 20.
The game ends when all 20 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player a set of six tokens.
flow.say: These cards show everyday changes. Each player has six tokens. We will guess which speed-up each card is about.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take six tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Speed-Up. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. The reader reads the front. Everyone puts a token face down. Turn them over together and read the back.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone chooses a token and puts it face down. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who got a point?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.
flow.context: In this step you play the first eight cards and learn how to guess.

ask.q: How did you choose your token on that card?
good: I looked for hot or cold.
I asked what makes particles meet more.
I looked for a helper that is not used up.

flow.do: Play the next twelve cards, or as many as you have time for. Keep score. Talk about any card where players chose different tokens.
flow.say: Keep going with the rest of the cards. If players chose different tokens for a card, talk about why before you read the back.
flow.kid: Play the rest of the cards. Talk about cards where you disagreed.
flow.context: In this step you play the rest of the cards and talk about any disagreements.
flow.parent: Some cards could fit more than one token. A pressure cooker is warmth, but also trapped steam. If a player can give a good reason for a different token, say so, and give a bonus point.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which card surprised them most, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card surprised you most? Why did it surprise you?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.context: This is the last step of Which Speed-Up. You look back at the game.
flow.think: Which speed-up do you think the kitchen at home uses most?

games.title: Meeting Party: be the particles
games.context: This is an act-out game. You and the other players are particles in a room. You find out what changes the number of meetings in 20 seconds.

setup.art: A tape square on a floor, about three steps on each side, with four children standing in it and one holding a phone timer.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a square on the floor with tape or string. Four players are particles. One counts.

setup.art: Two children shaking hands in the middle of the square while the counter makes a mark on paper.
setup.caption: 2. When two particles shake hands, that is one meeting. The counter makes a mark.

setup.art: Four children walking quickly in a smaller square, with more marks on the counter's sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Change the rules each round and count the meetings again.

printables.title: 4 round cards: the rule on the front, and what to expect on the back

items.f: Round 1. Walk slowly in the big square for 20 seconds. Shake hands whenever you meet someone.
items.b: This is the base round. Expect a few meetings. Write the number.

items.f: Round 2. Walk fast in the big square for 20 seconds. Shake hands whenever you meet someone.
items.b: Warmth. Fast particles meet more often. Expect more meetings than round 1.

items.f: Round 3. Walk slowly in a small square for 20 seconds. Shake hands whenever you meet someone.
items.b: More crowded. The same particles in less space meet more often. Expect more meetings than round 1.

items.f: Round 4. Walk slowly in the big square for 20 seconds, but with only two particles. Shake hands whenever you meet.
items.b: Fewer particles. Meetings are rare. Expect fewer meetings than round 1.

printables.title: Score sheet: Round, What changed, Meetings in 20 seconds
items: Round 1: slow, big square, four particles
Round 2: fast, big square, four particles
Round 3: slow, small square, four particles
Round 4: slow, big square, two particles

rules: You need at least five people: four particles and one counter. Use a phone or clock to time 20 seconds.
Mark a big square with tape or string, about four steps on each side. Mark a small square with about two steps on each side.
In every round, the particles walk about at random. Each time two particles meet and shake hands, that is one meeting. The counter makes a mark for each meeting.
Particles must not stand still, and must walk in straight lines until they meet someone or reach the edge.
Play the four rounds in order. Write the number of meetings after each one.
The counter guesses before each round whether it will have more, the same or fewer meetings than round 1. A right guess scores a point.
After four rounds, swap roles and play again. The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: Mark the big square and the small square. Choose four particles and one counter. Read the first round card aloud. Ask the counter to guess.
flow.say: You four are particles in a glass of water. You are the counter. Mark the squares. Round one: walk slowly in the big square, and shake hands each time you meet. Counter, how many meetings will there be?
flow.kid: Mark two squares. Four are particles. One counts. Guess the meetings.
flow.context: This is the first step of Meeting Party. You set up the squares and choose roles.
flow.parent: Use tape, string, a rope, or chalk if you have a courtyard. The big square can be larger if you have the space. Keep walking paths clear of furniture.

flow.do: Play round 1 and round 2. Time 20 seconds for each. Write the meetings in the score sheet. Ask the counter what changed between the rounds.
flow.say: Play round one, slowly. Count the meetings. Now play round two, fast. Count again. What changed between the rounds?
flow.kid: Play round 1 slowly. Then play round 2 fast. Count the meetings.
flow.context: In this step you play the first two rounds and see what speed does.

ask.q: Why were there more meetings when everyone walked fast?
good: Fast particles cover more ground.
They bump into more people.
Warmth makes particles faster.

flow.do: Play round 3 and round 4. Time 20 seconds for each. Write the meetings in the score sheet. Ask the counter what changed between the rounds.
flow.say: Play round three, in the small square. Count the meetings. Now play round four, with only two particles. Count again. What changed?
flow.kid: Play round 3 in the small square. Then play round 4 with two particles.
flow.context: In this step you play the last two rounds and see what crowding does.

ask.q: Why did a smaller square give more meetings?
good: The same particles were closer together.
They had less room to avoid each other.
A crowd meets more often.

flow.parent: Round 4 shows what happens when particles are scarce, as in a diluted mix. If the numbers do not follow the pattern, play the round again twice and take the average. Chance matters when there are only a few particles.

flow.do: Look at the score sheet. Ask which rounds matched the speed-ups for warmth and crowding. Swap roles if there is time.
flow.say: Look at the score sheet. Which round was warmth? Which was crowding? What would stirring look like in this game?
flow.kid: Look at the score sheet. Which round was warmth? Which was a crowd?
flow.context: This is the last step of Meeting Party. You link the game to the speed-ups.
flow.think: A catalyst helps a meeting work. How could you add a catalyst to this game?
flow.parent: Good ideas for a catalyst include a player standing in the middle who makes a handshake count double. Stirring could be a player who pushes particles into new places. Smaller pieces could be one particle split into two walkers.

experiments.title: Three Cups: does warmth hurry the fizz?
experiments.question: Does the same amount of fruit salt fizz faster in cold water, room-temperature water or warm water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which cup will stop fizzing first, and which last? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Every cup is the same size and has 150 millilitres of water and half a level teaspoon of fruit salt. Nobody stirs. The only thing that changes is the temperature of the water, so any difference in the fizzing time comes from the temperature. We do each cup twice, because one try can be a fluke. The room-temperature cup is the control.

materials.item: 3 clear glasses or tumblers of the same size, about 250 millilitres
fruit salt such as Eno, plain flavour, 3 sachets or enough for 3 level teaspoons
a half-teaspoon measure, and a cup or jug marked at 150 millilitres
ice cubes and cold water from the fridge
warm water: hot tap water or kettle water mixed with cold, so that you can hold the glass for 10 seconds
a phone or clock with a stopwatch, a tray to stand the glasses on, and the results table
a kitchen thermometer, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the warm water and checks that it is not too hot to hold. Do not drink the water from the test glasses. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.
experiments.record: Write the seconds for each try in the table. Work out the average for each cup. Then draw a bar for each cup, with the cup names along the bottom and seconds up the side.
experiments.context: In this experiment you find out whether warmth makes the same fizz finish faster. You time three cups of water at different temperatures.

setup.art: Three identical clear glasses in a row on a tray, labelled cold, room and warm, each with a measuring jug beside it showing 150 millilitres.
setup.caption: 1. Put 150 millilitres of water in each glass. Make one cold, one room-temperature and one warm.

setup.art: A hand holding a half-teaspoon of fruit salt over a glass, with a phone stopwatch showing 0:00 beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Get half a level teaspoon of fruit salt ready. Start the stopwatch the moment it touches the water.

setup.art: A glass with a stream of bubbles rising from white powder at the bottom, and a stopwatch showing 0:12.
setup.caption: 3. Watch the bubbles. Do not stir.

setup.art: A hand pressing stop on the stopwatch beside a glass with only a few small bubbles on the side, and the time written in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Stop the clock when no bubbles rise from the powder. Write the time down.

setup.art: A bar chart drawn on paper with three bars of different heights for the cold, room and warm glasses.
setup.caption: 5. After two tries for each glass, draw a bar for each.

flow.do: Show your child the three glasses and the fruit salt. Say what changes and what stays the same. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will fizz the same powder in three glasses of water. One is cold, one is room-temperature and one is warm. Which will stop fizzing first? Which will be last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three glasses of water. One cold, one room, one warm. Which stops fizzing first? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Three Cups test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Why do you think that glass will finish first?
good: Warm water makes things go faster.
The cold glass slows it down.
The powder dissolves quicker in warm water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the results table.

flow.do: A grown-up makes the three kinds of water. Cold water: add ice for 5 minutes, then take the ice out. Room water: use tap water. Warm water: mix hot and cold until you can hold the glass for 10 seconds. Put 150 millilitres in each glass.
flow.say: Cold water first. Chill it with ice for five minutes, then take the ice out. The room glass is plain tap water. For the warm glass, mix hot and cold water until the glass is comfortable to hold. Pour 150 millilitres into each.
flow.kid: A grown-up helps with the warm water. Pour 150 millilitres into each glass. Label them cold, room and warm.
flow.context: In this step you make the three kinds of water. They are the only thing that will be different.
flow.parent: If you have a thermometer, cold is about 5 to 10 degrees, room is about 25 to 30, and warm is about 45 to 50. Without a thermometer, use your hand. Cold should ache a little. Warm should feel like a warm bath. It must not be hot.

check.q: Why do we use exactly 150 millilitres of water in every glass?
options: So that only the temperature is different
So the glasses look the same
check.why: If one glass had more water, the powder would spread out more and take a different time. Keeping the water the same means any difference in time comes from the temperature. A wrong pick usually means the fair test idea is still new, so read the fair test box again.

flow.do: Start with the room glass. Tip half a level teaspoon of fruit salt into the water. Start the stopwatch at once. Do not stir. Stop it when no bubbles rise. Write down the seconds. Then do the cold glass, and then the warm glass.
flow.say: Tip in half a teaspoon of fruit salt, and start the stopwatch at the same moment. Do not stir. Watch the bubbles rise from the powder at the bottom. Stop the clock when they stop. Write the seconds in the table.
flow.kid: Tip in the powder. Start the stopwatch. Do not stir. Stop it when bubbles stop.
flow.context: In this step you time the fizz in each glass, one at a time.

ask.q: What do you notice about the bubbles in the first few seconds compared with the last few?
good: They come fast at the start.
They slow down near the end.
There are fewer bubbles at the end.

flow.parent: Use fresh water for the second try. Pour out the old water, rinse the glass, and use new water at the same temperature. Warm water cools quickly, so for the second try make it warm again. Tiny bubbles on the side of the glass do not count. Stop the clock when no bubbles rise from the powder.

flow.do: Check the table. Work out the average for each glass by adding the two tries and dividing by two. Draw a bar for each glass.
flow.say: Add the two tries for each glass and divide by two. That gives the average. Now draw one bar for each glass. Which bar is shortest?
flow.kid: Add two tries. Divide by two. Draw a bar for each glass.
flow.context: In this step you turn the numbers into a picture, so it is easy to compare.

check.q: The warm glass finished in 14 seconds and the cold glass in 56 seconds. How many times faster was the warm glass?
check.why: 56 divided by 14 is 4, so the warm glass was 4 times faster. A pick of 42 means subtracting, which gives how many seconds apart they were, not how many times faster.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why they think it happened. Then explain.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Three Cups test. You say what you found out.
flow.think: The powder and the water were the same in every glass. So what was different about the water particles in the warm glass?
flow.parent: A strong answer says the warm glass finished first and the cold glass last. After they say what they saw, explain: in warm water the particles move faster, so they meet more often and harder. The powder particles meet the water faster too. If the order was not warm, room, cold, say that is also a result. Check the water amounts and whether anyone stirred, and try again.

experiments.title: Apple Race: speed up and slow down browning
experiments.question: Which browns an apple fastest: a plain chunk, grated apple, a chunk dipped in lime juice, a chunk in the fridge, or a chunk dipped in hot water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which plate will turn brown first, and which will stay palest? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: All the apple pieces come from one apple, cut at the same time. Each plate gets the same amount of apple. Each plate is different from the plain chunk in one way only. The plain chunk is the control. Plate B has smaller pieces, C has lime juice, D is cold, and E has a hot dip.

materials.item: 1 apple, such as a Shimla apple. If your apple browns very slowly, use a ripe banana or a pear
5 small plates, labelled A to E
a knife and a grater, used by a grown-up
1 lime or lemon, squeezed, and a spoon
a cup of just-boiled water, and a spoon to lift the apple out
a fridge shelf
a clock, a pencil, and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts and grates the apple and handles the just-boiled water. Wash the apple first. Do not eat the pieces that have been in the hot water or left for 30 minutes.
experiments.record: At 10, 20 and 30 minutes, give each plate a colour score from 0 to 4. 0 is cream-white like a fresh cut. 1 is a faint tan. 2 is tan. 3 is brown. 4 is dark brown. Then draw a line for each plate.
experiments.context: In this experiment you race five pieces of apple to see which turns brown fastest. You find out what speeds browning up and what slows it down.

setup.art: A whole apple, a knife, a grater and five plates labelled A to E laid out on a table.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the apple. Make 4 equal chunks and grate a heap the same size.

setup.art: Plate A with a plain chunk, plate B with grated apple, plate C with a chunk rolled in lime juice.
setup.caption: 2. A is plain. B is grated. C is rolled in a spoon of lime juice.

setup.art: Plate D with a chunk going into a fridge, and plate E with a chunk being lifted out of a cup of just-boiled water with a spoon.
setup.caption: 3. D goes in the fridge. E is dipped in just-boiled water for 30 seconds, then lifted out.

setup.art: Five plates in a row with a clock showing 10 minutes and a child looking closely at the cut faces.
setup.caption: 4. Wait 10 minutes. Look at the cut faces and score the colour.

setup.art: A small colour scale from cream-white to dark brown with numbers 0 to 4, held beside a plate.
setup.caption: 5. Score again at 20 and 30 minutes.

flow.do: Show your child the five plates. Say what will be done to each one. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will cut one apple and treat five plates differently. A is plain. B is grated. C has lime juice. D goes in the fridge. E gets a hot dip. Which turns brown first? Which stays palest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five plates of apple. Which turns brown first? Which stays palest? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Apple Race. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Why do you think that plate will turn brown first?
good: It has more apple touching the air.
Plain apple has nothing slowing it down.
Grated pieces are small.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the guesses at the top of the table.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts four equal chunks of apple, about 2 centimetres wide. Grate one more chunk's worth onto plate B. Put a chunk on plate A. Roll a chunk in a spoon of lime juice and put it on C. Put a chunk on D. Dip a chunk in just-boiled water for 30 seconds on a spoon, and put it on E. Put D in the fridge. Set the clock.
flow.say: Cut all the pieces at the same moment. A is plain. B is grated. C is rolled in lime juice. D goes straight in the fridge. E gets 30 seconds in just-boiled water. Start the clock when everything is on its plate.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the apple. Set up plates A to E. Start the clock.
flow.context: In this step you set up the five plates. Everything starts at the same time.
flow.parent: The cut faces must all be fresh and start at the same time. Put plates A, B, C and E in the same spot, away from a fan. Do not wipe the pieces. If you have no fridge shelf, use a bowl of ice-cold water under a cover.

check.q: Why is plate A, the plain chunk, kept in the test?
options: So that we can compare the other plates with it
Because it is the biggest chunk
check.why: Plate A shows what the apple does on its own. The other plates are each changed in one way, so any difference from A comes from that change. A wrong pick usually means the idea of a control is still new.

flow.do: At 10 minutes, look at the cut face of each plate. Give each a score from 0 to 4 and write it in the table. Do the same at 20 and 30 minutes. Take plate D out of the fridge for a moment each time.
flow.say: At ten minutes, look at the cut faces. Give each plate a score from nought to four. Write it down. Do the same at twenty and thirty minutes. Which plate changes first?
flow.kid: Look closely at each plate. Score the colour from 0 to 4. Write it in the table.
flow.context: In this step you watch the apple change colour and score it each time.

ask.q: What do you notice about the grated apple compared with the chunk?
good: It goes brown faster.
It is darker already.
More of it touches the air.

flow.parent: If your apple is slow to brown, wait up to an hour and keep scoring. If nothing browns, try a banana. Write what you see, even if it is not what you guessed. The cold plate may only be a little paler than the plain one in 30 minutes. That is also a result.

flow.do: Draw a line graph. Put minutes along the bottom and colour score up the side. Draw one line for each plate, in a different colour.
flow.say: Draw a line graph. Minutes go along the bottom and the colour score goes up the side. One line for each plate. Which line climbs fastest?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each plate. Which line climbs fastest?
flow.context: In this step you turn the scores into a graph so you can compare the plates.

check.q: Plate B, the grated apple, is darker than plate A, the chunk, at 10 minutes. What best explains this?
options: Grated apple has much more surface touching the air
check.why: Browning needs the cut surface to meet oxygen from the air. Grating makes many tiny pieces, so far more surface meets the air. A pick of sweeter or warmer is a guess that does not match the test, because the grated apple came from the same apple at the same temperature.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain.
flow.say: What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think each plate changed as it did?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Apple Race. You say what you found out.
flow.think: Lime juice and a hot dip both kept the apple pale. Do you think they did it in the same way?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the grated apple browned fastest because of its large surface, and that cold, lime and heat each slowed it. After they say what they saw, explain: a cut apple has an enzyme that helps oxygen turn some of the apple's own chemicals brown. Small pieces mean more surface. Cold slows the particles. Lime juice is acidic, and the enzyme works poorly in acid. The hot dip breaks the enzyme, so it cannot help any more.

experiments.title: Same Lime, More Water: does a crowd speed up the fizz?
experiments.question: If the amount of lime juice is the same, does the fizz with baking soda finish faster when the juice is more crowded, or when it is mixed into lots of water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which glass will finish fizzing first, and which last? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Each glass has the same size and the same amount of baking soda. Each gets 2 teaspoons of the same lime juice, so the same number of acid particles. Only the water added is different. Glass A has none, glass B has 4 teaspoons and glass C has 12 teaspoons. So the acid is the same amount, but it is more or less crowded.

materials.item: 3 tall narrow glasses of the same size
3 level teaspoons of baking soda
1 fresh lime or lemon, squeezed, with the seeds taken out, to give at least 6 teaspoons of juice
a teaspoon, water, and 3 small cups to mix in
a ruler, a stopwatch, a tray, and the results table

experiments.safety: Keep lime juice out of eyes. Wash your hands after squeezing. Do not drink the fizz.
experiments.record: Write the foam height at 5 seconds and the time until the fizz stops for each glass. Then draw a bar for each glass.
experiments.context: In this experiment you keep the amount of acid the same, but crowd it into a small space or spread it out. You see whether a crowd of acid particles reacts faster.

setup.art: Three tall glasses on a tray, each with one level teaspoon of baking soda lying at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Put 1 level teaspoon of baking soda in each tall glass.

setup.art: Three small cups, each with 2 teaspoons of lime juice, the first with no water, the second with 4 teaspoons of water, and the third with 12 teaspoons of water.
setup.caption: 2. Mix 2 teaspoons of lime juice in each cup. Add 0, 4 and 12 teaspoons of water.

setup.art: A hand pouring a cup of lime mix quickly into a tall glass of baking soda while a stopwatch starts.
setup.caption: 3. Pour cup A into glass A in one go. Start the stopwatch.

setup.art: A ruler held beside a tall glass of foam, with a stopwatch showing 0:05.
setup.caption: 4. At 5 seconds, measure the foam height with the ruler.

setup.art: A tall glass where the foam has gone down and only a few bubbles remain, with a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 5. Stop the clock when the fizz stops. Then do glasses B and C.

flow.do: Show your child the three glasses and the three cups. Say what goes in each. Write down their guess and reason.
flow.say: All three glasses get the same amount of lime juice. The first has no extra water. The second has a little. The third has a lot. Which fizzes fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Same lime in every cup. More water in B and C. Which fizzes fastest? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Same Lime test. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Why do you think that glass will fizz fastest?
good: The lime is stronger there.
More acid is close to the baking soda.
In the watery cup, the acid is spread out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the guesses on the table. Both lime and baking soda are safe in the kitchen, but keep the glasses on a tray because the foam can spill.

flow.do: Put 1 level teaspoon of baking soda in each glass. In the three cups, put 2 teaspoons of lime juice. Add no water to cup A, 4 teaspoons to cup B and 12 teaspoons to cup C. Stir each cup once.
flow.say: Baking soda goes into each tall glass first. Now we mix the lime cups. All three get 2 teaspoons of juice. Cup A gets no water. Cup B gets 4 teaspoons. Cup C gets 12 teaspoons.
flow.kid: Put baking soda in each tall glass. Mix the lime cups. Add 0, 4 and 12 spoons of water.
flow.context: In this step you set up the glasses and the cups. Only the water is different.
flow.parent: Use level teaspoons and the same spoon every time. Seeds can block bubbles, so take them out. Keep all three cups ready before you start, so the test is the same for each.

check.q: Cups A, B and C all have 2 teaspoons of lime juice. What is different about the acid in them?
options: How much of it there is
check.why: The same amount of acid is spread through 2, 6 or 14 teaspoons of liquid. So the amount stays the same, but the crowding changes. A pick of 'how much' means the amount and the crowding are still being mixed up.

flow.do: For each glass, pour the cup in one go and start the stopwatch. At 5 seconds, measure the foam height. Stop the clock when the fizz stops. Write both numbers in the table. Rinse and dry the glasses before doing the next one.
flow.say: Pour the whole cup into the glass in one go and start the stopwatch. At five seconds, measure the foam. Stop the clock when the fizz stops. Write both numbers. Do glass A, then B, then C.
flow.kid: Pour fast. Start the clock. Measure the foam at 5 seconds. Stop when fizz stops.
flow.context: In this step you do the test for each glass and write down what you see.
flow.parent: Do not stir. Foam from baking soda and lime can be small, so look at the side of the glass. If you want to repeat each test twice, do it with fresh mixes. If all three finish together, that is a result too. Write it down and say why you think so.

flow.do: Draw a bar for each glass. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain.
flow.say: Draw a bar for each glass. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think the crowded lime was different?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each glass. Say what you thought, saw and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Same Lime test. You say what you found out.
flow.think: The lime juice is the same amount in all three cups. So what changed about how often acid particles meet baking soda particles?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the least watery glass fizzed hardest and finished first, and that in the watery glass the acid was spread out, so meetings were rarer. After they say what they saw, explain: more crowded particles meet more often, so the reaction is faster. The total gas is the same in all three, because the amount of acid is the same. If your order is different, check that each glass got the same baking soda and a single pour.

activities.title: Stir or Stand: does a spoon hurry the fizz?

materials.item: 2 glasses of the same size
fruit salt such as Eno, 2 level half-teaspoons
a spoon
a jug of room-temperature water, marked at 150 millilitres
a stopwatch, paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Do not drink the water from the test glasses.
activities.record: Write the seconds for each glass. Draw two bars, one for the still glass and one for the stirred glass.
activities.context: In this activity you find out if stirring makes a reaction finish sooner. You time two identical glasses of fizz, one stirred and one left still.

setup.art: Two glasses of room-temperature water, labelled still and stirred, with a spoon beside the stirred glass.
setup.caption: 1. Pour 150 millilitres of water into each glass.

setup.art: A child tipping half a teaspoon of fruit salt into the still glass, with a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Tip fruit salt into the still glass. Time it. Do not stir.

setup.art: A child tipping half a teaspoon of fruit salt into the stirred glass and swirling it with a spoon, with a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 3. Tip fruit salt into the stirred glass. Stir gently the whole time. Time it.

flow.do: Pour 150 millilitres of room-temperature water into two glasses. Ask your child to guess which will stop fizzing sooner, and why.
flow.say: Two glasses, same water, same powder. One gets stirred and one stays still. Which stops fizzing sooner? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two glasses. One stirred, one still. Which fizzes out sooner? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Stir or Stand. You guess before you test.

ask.q: Why might stirring change the time?
good: It mixes the powder with the water.
Fresh water reaches the powder.
The bubbles get carried away.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Both glasses must use the same water and the same half teaspoon of powder.

flow.do: Tip half a teaspoon of fruit salt into the still glass and start the stopwatch. Stop it when no bubbles rise. Write the time. Then do the same in the stirred glass, but stir gently with a spoon the whole time.
flow.say: Powder into the still glass, and start the clock. Stop it when the bubbles stop. Now powder into the stirred glass. Stir gently the whole time. Time it the same way.
flow.kid: Tip in the powder. Time the still glass. Then time the stirred glass, stirring the whole time.
flow.context: In this step you time both glasses, one at a time.
flow.parent: Stir gently with the spoon in slow circles, not hard. Stop the clock when no bubbles rise, even if bubbles still cling to the spoon. If you want to do each twice, use fresh water.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain.
flow.say: What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think stirring made a difference?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of Stir or Stand. You say what you found out.
flow.think: Stirring does not make the water warmer or the powder smaller. So how can it make a reaction finish sooner?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the stirred glass finished sooner. After they say what they saw, explain: stirring keeps bringing fresh water to the powder and carrying the used-up water away, so more meetings happen each second. Stirring does not make particles faster. It brings new partners to the meeting. If the glasses finished together, say that is also a result and try again with a firmer stir.

activities.title: Helper Hunt at Home: where are the catalysts?

materials.item: a bottle or packet of washing powder or liquid, and one of dishwash or floor cleaner
paper and a pencil
a grown-up who drives or rides a vehicle, or who knows a mechanic

activities.safety: Do not open or taste any cleaner. Read labels only. Do not go under a vehicle. Ask a grown-up to look.
activities.record: Make a table with three columns: Where I looked, What I found, Which reaction the helper speeds up.
activities.context: In this activity you hunt for catalysts in your own home. You read labels, ask a driver, and think about your own body.

setup.art: A child reading the ingredient list on a washing powder packet, with a finger on the word enzymes.
setup.caption: 1. Read the label of a washing powder or liquid. Find the word enzyme.

setup.art: A child talking to an adult next to a parked car, with a pipe running under the car drawn in dotted lines.
setup.caption: 2. Ask a driver if the vehicle has a catalytic converter in its exhaust pipe.

setup.art: A child's mouth with a spoon of plain rice and an arrow to the word saliva enzyme.
setup.caption: 3. Think of the helpers inside you, such as the enzyme in your saliva.

flow.do: Look at the label of a washing powder or washing liquid. Find words such as enzymes, protease, amylase, lipase or cellulase. Write down what you find. Do the same for dishwash or floor cleaner.
flow.say: Let us hunt for helpers. Many washing powders say enzymes on the label. Look for the words enzyme, protease, amylase, lipase or cellulase. Write down what you find, even if you find nothing.
flow.kid: Read the washing powder label. Look for the word enzyme. Write what you find.
flow.context: This is the first step of Helper Hunt. You look for enzymes on a label.

ask.q: Why would a washing powder want an enzyme in it?
good: To break down stains faster.
To clean without hot water.
A helper speeds up the job.

flow.parent: Protease breaks down proteins such as egg and blood stains. Amylase breaks down starch such as rice and potato. Lipase breaks down fats such as oil. Cellulase works on the fibres in cotton. If the label does not say, that is also a result.

flow.do: Ask a grown-up who drives if their vehicle has a catalytic converter. Ask them to find out if they are not sure. Write down what they say.
flow.say: Ask someone who drives, or a mechanic. Does the vehicle have a catalytic converter in the exhaust? Petrol cars in India are made with one. Write down what they say.
flow.kid: Ask a driver about the exhaust helper. Write down the answer.
flow.context: In this step you find out about the helper in a vehicle's exhaust pipe.
flow.parent: A catalytic converter is a metal honeycomb coated with thin layers of metals such as platinum, palladium and rhodium. It changes harmful gases such as carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide. It works best when hot, so the first minute after a cold start is the dirtiest. Do not let your child go under the vehicle.

check.q: A catalytic converter helps harmful gases change into safer gases. What happens to the metal in the converter?
options: It stays, ready to help again
It is used up and must be refilled each week
It turns into the safer gas
