check.why: A catalyst is not used up. The metal in the converter helps again and again, and lasts for years. A pick of used up means the idea of a catalyst is still being mixed with ordinary ingredients.

flow.do: Ask your child to think of helpers in their own body. Chew a spoon of plain rice for one minute and say what changes in the taste. Then fill the third column of the table.
flow.say: Your mouth has a helper too. Chew a spoon of plain rice for a whole minute. Does the taste change? Then fill in the last column of the table.
flow.kid: Chew plain rice for one minute. Does it get sweet? Fill in the table.
flow.context: In this step you meet a helper in your own mouth, and finish the table.
flow.think: A catalyst speeds up one job and comes out the same. What jobs do you think the helpers in your body might be doing?
flow.parent: Saliva has an enzyme called amylase that breaks starch into sugar. Plain rice may begin to taste a little sweet after a minute. Some children do not notice, and that is fine. After they have shared, explain that a catalyst speeds up one job and is not used up.

activities.title: Kitchen Clock: why does the pressure cooker hurry the dal?

materials.item: a family cook or grown-up who cooks, and some cooking they are doing anyway
paper, a pencil and a clock

activities.safety: Stay away from the hot stove and from the cooker when it whistles. A grown-up does all the cooking.
activities.record: Make a table with four columns: Food, How it was prepared, Minutes to cook, Which speed-up helped.
activities.context: In this activity you interview the cook at home about cooking times. You find out which speed-ups the kitchen already uses.

setup.art: A child with a notebook asking a person who is stirring a pot on a stove in a kitchen.
setup.caption: 1. Ask the cook how long dal takes in an open pot and in a pressure cooker.

setup.art: A table with columns Food, How prepared, Minutes and Speed-up, with a few rows already filled in.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in a row for each food, such as dal, potato cubes and a whole potato.

setup.art: A pressure cooker with a whistle on a stove, and an arrow to a thermometer reading 120 degrees.
setup.caption: 3. Think about which speed-up each food uses.

flow.do: Ask the cook how long dal takes to cook in an open pot, and how long it takes in a pressure cooker. Write both times in a table. Ask why they use the cooker.
flow.say: Ask the cook at home. How long does dal take in an open pot? How long does it take in the pressure cooker? Write both numbers down. Why do they use the cooker?
flow.kid: Ask the cook about dal. Open pot or cooker? How many minutes?
flow.context: This is the first step of Kitchen Clock. You ask the cook for the times.

ask.q: Why do you think the pressure cooker is quicker?
good: It gets hotter than an open pot.
The steam is trapped inside.
It pushes the heat into the dal.

flow.parent: If your family does not use a cooker, ask about another food, such as whole rajma versus soaked rajma. In an open pot, water boils at 100 degrees. In a pressure cooker, trapped steam builds up pressure, and the water reaches about 115 to 120 degrees. That is hotter, so the food cooks faster.

flow.do: Add three more rows to the table. Ask about potato cubes and a whole potato. Ask about soaked and unsoaked chana. Ask about a split dal and a whole dal. Write the minutes in each row.
flow.say: Now add more rows. How long do potato cubes take, compared with a whole potato? How long does soaked chana take, compared with dry chana? Write each time down.
flow.kid: Add rows. Cubes or whole? Soaked or dry? Write the minutes.
flow.context: In this step you collect more cooking times to compare.
flow.parent: Expect cubes to cook faster than a whole potato because they have more surface for the heat to enter. Soaking lets water into the chana before cooking, so the chana cooks faster. Split dal cooks faster than whole dal for the same reason. Let your child choose the foods if the family cooks something else.

flow.do: Go down the table with your child. For each row, ask which speed-up the cook used: warmth, smaller pieces or something else. Write it in the last column.
flow.say: Look at each row. Which speed-up helped here? Was it more warmth, smaller pieces, or something else? Write it in the last column.
flow.kid: For each food, name the speed-up. Write it down.
flow.context: In this step you match each food to the speed-up that helped.
flow.think: Where in your kitchen could you slow a change down, to make food last longer?
flow.parent: Good answers include the pressure cooker for warmth, cubes and split dal for smaller pieces, and soaking for letting water in. Stirring and a hotter flame also count. Ask what the family does to slow things down, such as the fridge, a lid or a pickle.

projects.title: Rust Race: five nails, five conditions

materials.item: 5 plain iron nails, not galvanised. Ask the hardware shop for bright wire nails
5 clear glasses or jars of the same size
salt, a teaspoon, water, and a spoon
a little cooking oil, on a cotton bud
clear nail polish or a little paint, applied by a grown-up
a piece of tissue paper and a small lid or saucer
a pencil, paper, labels and the results table

projects.safety: A grown-up applies the nail polish or paint, in a place with fresh air. Nails are sharp. Wash your hands after touching rusty nails, and never touch them if you have a cut.

schedule.what: Set up the five nails and write down your guess.
Look at each nail. Score the rust from 0 to 4.
Look again, score again and take a photo or draw each nail.
Score a last time. Draw a line graph and say what you found.

projects.record: Score each nail each day from 0 (bright and clean) to 4 (covered in orange-brown rust, with flakes). Draw a line graph with one line for each nail.
projects.context: In this project you watch five nails over four days. You see how water, salt, oil and paint speed up or slow down rusting.

setup.art: Five glasses labelled A to E on a tray, each with a bright iron nail in a different condition.
setup.caption: 1. Set up five glasses. A is dry, B has plain water, C has salty water, D has an oiled nail in water, and E has a painted nail in water.

setup.art: A hand rubbing a bright nail with soap and a cloth, then drying it.
setup.caption: 2. Wash each nail with soap, and dry it. Do not touch the washed nails with oily hands.

setup.art: A child looking at a nail in salty water, with a faint orange cloud around it.
setup.caption: 3. Look each day. Score the rust from 0 to 4.

setup.art: A line graph on paper with five lines going up at different speeds.
setup.caption: 4. On day 4, draw a line graph of the five scores.

flow.do: Wash and dry all five nails. Put nail A on a dry tissue in a glass. For B, C, D and E, stand the nail in a glass with water that covers half the nail. Add 2 teaspoons of salt to C. A grown-up paints nail E before it goes in, and lets it dry. Rub a little oil on nail D. Write your guess for each glass.
flow.say: Five nails, five conditions. A is dry. B is in plain water. C is in salty water. D is oiled and in water. E is painted and in water. Which will rust first? Which will not rust at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Set up five nails. Guess which rusts first and which not at all. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rust Race. You set up the glasses and guess.

ask.q: Why do you think that nail will rust first?
good: Salt helps rusting.
Water and air both touch it.
It has nothing protecting it.

flow.parent: Put the glasses on a tray in a place where they will not be knocked. Keep the tissue dry in glass A. Use the same amount of water in B, C, D and E. The nail in the middle of the water rusts most near the water line, where it meets both water and air.

flow.do: Each day, look at each nail and score the rust from 0 to 4. Write the scores in the table. Do not shake the glasses.
flow.say: Look at each nail every day. Give each one a rust score from nought to four. Write it down. Do not shake the glasses.
flow.kid: Look at each nail. Score the rust from 0 to 4.
flow.context: In this step you check the nails each day and write down the scores.
flow.wait: Check once a day, for three days
flow.parent: Salty water usually shows orange rust within a day. Plain water takes longer, often two or three days. A dry nail, a well-oiled nail and a fully painted nail may show no rust at all. If a spot of paint chipped, rust may start there. Write what you see, even if it is not what you guessed.

flow.do: On day 4, score the nails for the last time. Draw the line graph. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain.
flow.say: Draw a line for each nail. Which line climbs fastest? Which stays flat? What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each nail. Say what you thought, saw and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Rust Race. You say what you found out.
flow.think: Salty water and paint have opposite effects. What is each one doing to the meeting between iron, water and oxygen?
flow.parent: A strong answer says salt speeds up rusting, and oil and paint slow it by keeping the iron from water and air. After they say what they saw, explain: rusting is iron meeting oxygen and water. Salt dissolved in the water helps electric charge move around, so rusting is faster. Oil and paint are barriers that keep the meeting from happening. The Delhi Iron Pillar has a thin skin that is a natural barrier of this kind.

challenges.title: Tiffin Apple: keep cut apple pale until lunch
challenges.problem: A cut apple goes brown in a school tiffin box before lunch. Design a way to keep cut apple slices pale for at least four hours, using only things from your kitchen. Your design should not change the taste too much.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
Do not use any chemicals from a shop other than food.
Test at least two designs and one plain control.
The slices must be safe to eat at the end if they have not been in hot water.
materials: 1 apple, cut into slices by a grown-up
a small tiffin box with a lid
cling film or a piece of banana leaf
an ice pack or a frozen bottle
general: Dip the slices in lime juice for 10 seconds, and shake off the extra.
Dip the slices in lightly salted water, about a quarter teaspoon of salt in a cup of water, for one minute.
Pack the slices tightly together in a box with a lid, and put an ice pack next to the box.
creative: Put the slices back together into the shape of an apple, and wrap the whole thing in cling film so little air gets to the cut faces.
Dip the slices in a little diluted honey water, a teaspoon of honey in a cup of water.
Keep the whole apple uncut in the tiffin and cut it at lunchtime with a small safe knife. This avoids the problem altogether.
challenges.your_turn: Pick two designs and a plain control. Make three small boxes. At 1 hour, 2 hours and 4 hours, score the colour from 0 to 4. Which design worked best, and what was it keeping apart or slowing down?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about slowing a reaction down. You use what you learned in the Apple Race to keep cut apple pale.

setup.art: Three small tiffin boxes labelled plain, lime and sealed, each with apple slices inside, and an ice pack beside the box labelled sealed.
setup.caption: 1. Make three boxes. One is plain, and two have a design.

setup.art: A child holding a card with colour scores from 0 to 4 beside a box of apple slices.
setup.caption: 2. After 1, 2 and 4 hours, open a box and score the colour.

flow.do: Look at the Apple Race results. Ask your child which things slowed the browning. Ask them to choose two designs to test, and to guess which will work better.
flow.say: In the Apple Race, which things slowed the browning? Pick two of them, or two of your own ideas. Which will keep the apple pale longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which things slowed the browning? Pick two designs. Which is best? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tiffin Apple challenge. You choose two designs and guess.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the apple into slices. Make three boxes with the same number of slices in each. Box A is plain. Boxes B and C get the two designs. Label the boxes and write down the time.
flow.say: Make three boxes with the same number of slices. A is plain. B has your first design. C has your second design. Label them and write down the time.
flow.kid: Make three boxes. A is plain. B and C have your designs.
flow.context: In this step you build your designs and the plain control.
flow.parent: Keep the boxes together on a shelf, away from the fridge, so that A, B and C are in the same room. If a design includes a cold pack, keep it next to the box and not touching the apple. Salty water must be only lightly salty.

flow.do: At 1 hour, 2 hours and 4 hours, open each box and score the colour from 0 to 4. Write the scores down. At the end, ask your child which design was best and why.
flow.say: At one, two and four hours, open each box and give the apple a score from nought to four. Write it down. Which design worked best? What was it doing to the browning reaction?
flow.kid: Open each box at 1, 2 and 4 hours. Score the colour. Which design won?
flow.context: In this step you test your designs and score them.
flow.think: If you had to keep apple pale for two days, what would you try?
flow.parent: Lime juice and cold usually keep apple pale the longest. A sealed box with little air helps because the cut faces meet less oxygen. If your control stayed pale for four hours, the apple may be a slow-browning kind. Try a banana or another fruit. Do not eat slices that look or smell wrong.

worksheets.title: Fast, Slow and the Four Speed-Ups (core)

items.p: What happens in a chemical reaction?
opts: Particles of different substances meet and rearrange into new substances
A substance only changes its shape
A solid always turns into a liquid
items.why: A reaction makes new substances, because particles meet and rearrange. Changing shape or state, like ice melting, makes no new substance. A wrong pick often means a change of state is being mixed up with a reaction.

items.p: A sachet of dry fruit salt fizzes by itself while it sits closed on a shelf.
items.why: False. The powders are dry, so their particles cannot move and meet. Water lets them dissolve and mix, and then they react.

items.p: Fruit salt fizzes in water. What are the bubbles?
opts: Carbon dioxide gas, a new substance
Air that was trapped in the powder
Steam from the water
items.why: Baking soda and citric acid react and make carbon dioxide. Trapped air would not keep coming for half a minute, and the water is not hot enough to make steam.

items.p: Sort these changes into fast (seconds or minutes) and slow (days or longer).
items: fruit salt fizzing in warm water
items.why: A cracker, fizz and hot tea finish in seconds. Rust, yellow paper and pickles change over days, months or years. A strong answer says each one is a reaction, just at a different rate.

items.p: Match each speed-up to an example.
pairs: Sugar dissolving faster in hot tea
A spoon swirling a glass of fizz
Strong vinegar fizzing harder than weak vinegar
items.why: Warmth means faster particles. Stirring brings fresh partners. Smaller pieces give more surface. A crowd means more particles per space. All four make meetings more frequent or stronger.

items.p: When water gets warmer, its particles move ____.
items.why: Temperature measures how fast particles move. In warm water they move faster, so they meet more often and harder.

items.p: In the chart, which glass finished fizzing first?
opts: The warm glass
The cold glass
The room glass
items.why: The warm glass has the shortest bar, 15 seconds. A shorter time means a faster reaction. A wrong pick often means a tall bar was read as faster.

chart.title: Fizz times for fruit salt in three glasses (a made-up example)

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Hyderabad, times fruit salt in two glasses. The cold glass takes 90 seconds. The warm glass takes 30 seconds. How many times faster is the warm glass?
items.why: 90 divided by 30 is 3. The warm glass finished 3 times faster. Subtracting would only tell you how many seconds apart they were.

items.p: Stirring makes the particles in a liquid move faster.
items.why: False. Stirring does not speed up particles. It brings fresh partners to a meeting and carries used-up liquid away.

items.p: Zoya says a heap of fine powder reacts faster than one big lump of the same stuff. Explain why she is right, using the word surface.
items.a: A lump only reacts where its surface touches the other substance. Powder has many tiny pieces, so its total surface is much larger. More of the stuff can meet the other substance at once, so the reaction is faster.
items.why: A strong answer names the surface, says more of it touches the other substance, and links that to faster reactions. It may also mention the grated apple.

items.p: Draw two glasses of water side by side, one cold and one warm. Draw dots for particles and arrows to show how fast they move.
items.a: Two glasses with dots in each. Short arrows on the dots in the cold glass and long arrows on the dots in the warm glass.
items.why: A strong drawing shows longer arrows in the warm glass, because its particles move faster. Some also mark more bumps in the warm glass.

items.p: What is special about a catalyst?
opts: It speeds up a reaction and is not used up
It is the ingredient that makes the most product
It slows a reaction down
items.why: A catalyst comes out the same as it went in, so it can work again. It is not an ingredient. A pick of slows down means it was mixed up with the idea of a slow-down, such as a fridge.

items.p: Three of these slow a change down. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: A fridge
A coat of paint
Stirring
Lime juice on cut apple
items.why: A fridge cools, paint blocks the meeting, and lime juice slows the browning enzyme. Stirring brings fresh partners together, so it speeds a reaction up.

items.p: Put these changes in order from the fastest to the slowest.
items: fruit salt fizzing in warm water
a: fruit salt fizzing in warm water
items.why: A cracker bangs in a flash. The warm fizz takes about 15 seconds. An apple browns in minutes to hours. A gate rusts over months. All four are reactions at different rates.

items.p: A family is arguing about how to keep sliced apple pale in a tiffin box.

views.says: Squeeze lime juice on the slices. The acid slows the browning.
Put the slices in lightly salted water for a minute, and then pack them.
Don't cut the apple until lunch. Then it has no time to brown.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses an idea from the unit, such as that lime juice makes the enzyme work poorly, or that an uncut apple has less surface meeting air. It also names one good point from another view.
items.why: All three ideas keep oxygen, the enzyme and the cut surface apart or slow. A strong answer gives a reason, not just a choice.

items.p: A graph of fizz against time rises steeply at first and then flattens. What does the flat part mean?
opts: One of the reactants has been used up, so no more gas is made
The reaction has become boring
The water has become cold
items.why: At the start there are many fresh particles to meet, so the rate is high. As they are used up, fewer meetings happen. When one reactant runs out, the curve goes flat.

items.p: Here is a curve of gas made against time. Label the three parts: 'steep: many fresh particles', 'bending over: fewer left' and 'flat: one reactant used up'.
a: The first part of the curve is steep
items.why: The steep start is the highest rate. As reactants are used up, the curve bends over. When one runs out, it goes flat.
items.art: A curve with seconds along the bottom and gas up the side. It rises steeply at the start, bends in the middle and flattens at the end. Three empty label boxes sit beside the three parts.

items.p: A cube of jaggery has sides of 3 centimetres. Each face is 9 square centimetres, and a cube has 6 faces. What is its total surface area in square centimetres?
items.why: 6 faces times 9 square centimetres is 54. Cut into smaller cubes, the same jaggery would have much more surface area.

items.p: A reaction takes 40 minutes at 20 degrees. For each 10 degrees warmer it takes half the time. How many minutes will it take at 40 degrees?
items.why: At 30 degrees it takes half of 40, which is 20 minutes. At 40 degrees it takes half of 20, which is 10 minutes. This is a rule of thumb, not an exact law.

items.p: A catalyst is ____ used up by the reaction it speeds up.
items.why: A catalyst comes out unchanged, so the same potato, or the same exhaust metal, can help again and again.

items.p: A catalyst changes how much product you finally get from the same amount of reactants.
items.why: False. A catalyst only changes how fast the product forms. The final amount depends on how much reactant you started with.

items.p: Why can a washing powder with enzymes lift food stains even in cool water?
opts: Enzymes are catalysts that work without needing high heat
Enzymes heat the water
Enzymes are scrubbed away with the stain
items.why: Enzymes are catalysts. They lower the effort the reaction needs, so the stain breaks down quickly without hot water. A pick of heating the water confuses a catalyst with a heater.

items.p: Sort each of these by what it does to a reaction.
items.why: Stirring, powder and the hotter cooker make meetings more frequent or stronger. A fridge, acid and paint make them rarer or weaker.

items.p: Match each way of slowing a change to an example.
pairs: A hot dip for an apple chunk
items.why: Each one slows the change by a different route. Cold slows the particles, paint keeps the iron from water and air, acid makes the enzyme work poorly, and the hot dip destroys the enzyme.

items.p: A hot dip of just-boiled water keeps a cut apple pale. Why?
opts: The heat breaks the browning enzyme, so it cannot help any more
The heat makes the apple wet
The heat cools the apple
items.why: Enzymes are folded chains that fall apart in strong heat. Without the enzyme, the browning reaction is far slower. A wrong pick often means heat is thought to always speed things up.

items.p: Salty water makes a nail rust faster than plain water. Explain why salt might help, and say how you could test it with three glasses.
items.a: Salt dissolved in the water helps electric charge move, which speeds up rusting. To test it, put the same kind of nail in plain water, in salty water and in dry air, then score the rust each day.
items.why: A strong answer says salt speeds rusting, gives a reason or says it helps charge move, and describes a fair test with one change and a control.

items.p: Draw a mountain with a high path over the top and a low tunnel through it. Label the high path 'no catalyst' and the tunnel 'with catalyst', and draw walkers coming out the other end.
items.a: A mountain with a path over the top and a tunnel through it. Labels on each. Walkers coming out at the far end of both.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tunnel as an easier route to the same place. The walkers and the destination are the same with and without the tunnel.

items.p: Old glass windows have flowed downwards over the centuries, which is why they are thicker at the bottom.
items.why: False. Calculations show glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow that much. Old panes were uneven when they were made.

items.p: A lump of flour does not explode, but a cloud of fine flour dust can. What is the best reason?
opts: Dust has far more surface touching the air, so it burns almost all at once
Dust is hotter than a lump
Dust is a different substance
items.why: A lump burns only on its outside. Fine dust spreads out in the air, so almost every bit meets oxygen at the same time. A pick of a different substance means surface is not yet linked to rate.

items.p: Two visitors are talking about the Delhi Iron Pillar, which has rusted very little in about 1,600 years.

views.says: The pillar must be made of some special iron that does not want to rust.
The iron is ordinary in this way. A thin skin that stays stuck keeps water and air away from the iron below.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with more? Give a reason from this unit, and say what you could test.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and gives a reason. For example, a bare nail that makes a skin that stays on rusts slowly, while flaking rust lets rusting go on. It might suggest comparing a nail with a stuck-on coat and a nail without.
items.why: Scientists found a thin protective skin on the pillar, which supports Gauri's idea. The iron also has a lot of phosphorus, so both ideas have a part of the truth.

items.p: A pot of dal needs to cook faster. Give three different ways to speed it up, and say which speed-up each one uses.
items.a: Use a pressure cooker, which uses warmth because it makes the water hotter than 100 degrees. Soak the dal first so water is already inside. Use split dal or mash it, which gives smaller pieces and more surface. Stirring can also help.
items.why: A strong answer names three ideas and links each to meetings: warmth for faster particles, small pieces for more surface, soaking for water already inside, stirring for fresh partners.

items.p: Three glasses each get 2 teaspoons of lime juice, mixed with 0, 4 or 12 teaspoons of water, and then all are poured onto plenty of baking soda. At the end, how does the total gas compare?
opts: It is about the same, because the amount of acid is the same
The glass with the most water makes the most gas
The glass with no water makes the most gas
items.why: Total gas depends on how much acid there was, not how crowded it was. Crowding changes how fast the gas is made. A wrong pick means speed and amount are being mixed up.

items.p: In a glass, 2 teaspoons of lime juice are mixed with 4 teaspoons of water. What fraction of the liquid is lime juice?
items.why: The total is 2 plus 4, which is 6 teaspoons. Two out of six is one third. The more water you add, the smaller this fraction, and the less crowded the acid.

items.p: A catalyst is added to a reaction that would finally make 10 grams of product. How much product does it finally make?
opts: 10 grams, but it makes it faster
20 grams, because a catalyst doubles the product
5 grams, because the catalyst uses some
items.why: A catalyst is not an ingredient. It only speeds up the change, and the amount of product depends on the reactants. A pick of 20 means a catalyst is thought to make more stuff.

items.p: Dipping a cut apple chunk in just-boiled water makes it brown faster, because heat speeds up everything.
items.why: False. Heat speeds up many reactions, but it also breaks the browning enzyme. Without the enzyme, the chunk stays pale.

items.p: A fridge slows down the spoiling of milk but does not stop it. Explain this using particles and meetings.
items.a: In the cold, the particles in milk move more slowly, so they meet less often and less hard. Fewer meetings work, so spoiling goes slowly. But some meetings still work, so the milk still changes in time.
items.why: A strong answer says slow particles meet less often and less hard, and that a few meetings still work, so cold slows a change but does not stop it.

items.p: Hydrogen peroxide is sold in a dark brown bottle. Why?
opts: Light speeds up its breakdown, so the dark bottle slows it down
The brown colour makes it cold
Brown plastic is cheaper
items.why: Light gives energy that speeds the breakdown of peroxide. A dark bottle keeps light out, so the change goes slowly and the peroxide lasts longer.

items.p: Three of these are catalysts. Which one is the odd one out because it is used up?
opts: Platinum in a car's exhaust
Catalase in a potato
Iron in an ammonia factory
Vinegar poured on baking soda
items.why: The metal in the exhaust, the potato's catalase and the iron in the factory all help again and again. Vinegar is a reactant. It is used up when it reacts with the baking soda.

items.p: Put these glasses in order from the most crowded lime juice to the least crowded.
items: 2 teaspoons of lime juice in 14 teaspoons of mix
2 teaspoons of lime juice in 2 teaspoons of mix
2 teaspoons of lime juice in 6 teaspoons of mix
a: 2 teaspoons of lime juice in 2 teaspoons of mix
2 teaspoons of lime juice in 6 teaspoons of mix
2 teaspoons of lime juice in 14 teaspoons of mix
items.why: The same lime juice is in less liquid in the first one, so its acid is most crowded. The more water, the more spread out it is.

items.p: To find the speed of a reaction, we measure how much new substance forms in each ____ or minute.
items.why: Speed is an amount per time. A firework and a rusting pillar can both be measured this way, with different units of time.

items.p: Here is a picture of an arrow with particles. Label the starting particles 'reactants', the new particles 'products' and the particle that comes out unchanged 'catalyst'.
a: The starting particles on the left are the reactants
the new particles on the right are the products
the helper that appears on both sides is the catalyst
items.why: Reactants are used up. Products are new. The catalyst helps and comes out unchanged, so it appears on both sides of the arrow.
items.art: A reaction arrow with two kinds of dots on the left, a different kind of dots on the right, and a small star-shaped helper particle drawn above the arrow and again unchanged on the right.

items.p: Draw one graph with two curves for gas made against time: one for fruit salt in warm water and one in cold water. Label which is which.
items.a: Two curves that rise and flatten at the same final height, the warm one rising steeply and flattening sooner, the cold one rising gently and flattening later.
items.why: Both glasses make the same final amount of gas, because the powder is the same. The warm curve is steeper and flattens sooner, because its rate is higher.

items.p: Diamond is always very slowly turning into graphite, but a diamond ring seems to stay the same forever. Why?
opts: The rate is so low that no change is visible in a lifetime
The change has stopped completely
Diamonds are alive and repair themselves
items.why: Slow does not mean stopped. The meetings that would change diamond are extremely rare. A wrong pick means slow and still are being mixed up.

items.p: A grown mayfly may live for only one day. A person lives for decades. A mountain lasts for millions of years. They are watching an iron gate rust.

views.says: The gate never changes. It looks exactly the same all day.
The gate changes slowly. In a few years it is covered in rust.
The gate is gone in a blink, like a cracker banging.

items.ask: Is 'slow' something about the change, or something about the one who is watching? Give a reason, and say what could settle it.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it. For example, slow is measured against a clock, and we can measure a rate in amount per time without a watcher. But whether it looks slow depends on how long the watcher lives. It could mention measuring rate with a clock.
items.why: Both parts have something right. A rate can be measured as an amount per time, so it is about the change. Whether we call it fast or slow depends on the one watching.

items.p: Choose one thing at home that rusts, spoils or browns. Say which speed-up or slow-down you would use on it, and explain how it works using meetings of particles.
items.a: An answer might choose cut apple, and say lime juice slows the browning enzyme, or choose an iron grill and say paint keeps water and oxygen away from the iron. It should say that the particles meet less often or less strongly.
items.why: A strong answer picks a real thing, names a slow-down or speed-up, and ties it to meetings: fewer, rarer or weaker meetings slow a change, and more or stronger meetings speed it up.

quiz.p: What has to happen before two substances can react?
opts: Their particles must meet
They must be the same colour
One must be a liquid
quiz.why: A reaction is a meeting. Dry fruit salt does nothing until water lets its particles move and meet. A wrong pick often means a property of the substance is mistaken for the cause.

quiz.p: Why does the same fruit salt finish fizzing sooner in warm water?
opts: Warm water has faster particles that meet more often and harder
Warm water has more fruit salt in it
Warm water makes the powder lighter
quiz.why: Temperature measures how fast particles move. Faster particles meet more often and more forcefully. The amount of powder is the same in every glass.

quiz.p: Why does grated apple turn brown faster than one big chunk?
opts: More of the apple is touching the air
Grated apple is sweeter
Grated apple is warmer
quiz.why: Browning happens where cut apple meets oxygen. Grating makes many tiny pieces, so far more surface meets the air.

quiz.p: Which of these is a catalyst?
opts: Catalase in a potato, helping hydrogen peroxide break down
Baking soda poured on vinegar
Lime juice on a cut apple
quiz.why: Catalase speeds up the breakdown of peroxide and is not used up. Baking soda is used up in the fizz. Lime juice slows a reaction down.

quiz.p: What is the best way to slow down the rusting of an iron gate?
opts: Cover it with paint, so water and air cannot reach it
Leave it in salty air
Wash it with vinegar
quiz.why: Rusting needs iron to meet water and oxygen. Paint keeps them apart. Salty air and vinegar speed rusting up.

quiz.p: The same lime juice is mixed with more water. What happens to the speed of its fizz on baking soda?
opts: It slows down, because the acid is less crowded
It speeds up, because there is more liquid
It stays the same
quiz.why: The same acid spread through more water is less crowded, so meetings with baking soda are rarer. The final amount of gas stays the same.

quiz.p: A graph of gas made against time rises steeply and then flattens. What does the steep part show?
opts: The reaction is fastest at the start
The reaction has stopped
A catalyst was added
quiz.why: At the start there are plenty of fresh particles to meet, so the rate is highest. It slows as they are used up.

quiz.p: A cut apple dipped in just-boiled water stays pale, because the heat breaks the ____ that helps it turn brown.
quiz.why: Enzymes are folded chains that fall apart in strong heat. With the enzyme broken, browning is far slower.

quiz.p: The Delhi Iron Pillar has rusted very little in about 1,600 years. What best explains this?
opts: A thin, tightly stuck skin keeps water and air from the iron below
Iron never rusts in Delhi
The pillar is made of a metal that cannot react
quiz.why: Scientists found a thin protective skin on the pillar. The iron itself can react, but it rarely meets water and air. A wrong pick treats the iron as magic instead of looking at the meeting.

quiz.p: Putting food in a fridge stops every change in it.
quiz.why: False. Cold only slows the particles, so meetings are rarer and weaker. The changes continue, but slowly.

quiz.p: Pooja, a girl in Kochi, finds a fizz takes 48 seconds in cold water and 12 seconds in warm water. How many times faster is the warm fizz?
quiz.why: 48 divided by 12 is 4. The warm fizz is 4 times faster. Subtracting would give how many seconds apart they are.

quiz.p: Stirring a glass of fizz makes it finish sooner. What does stirring do?
opts: It brings fresh water to the powder
It makes the particles hotter
It makes the powder bigger
quiz.why: Stirring does not change the temperature or the size of the powder. It carries used-up liquid away and brings fresh partners to the meeting.

applications: Pressure cookers cook dal and rice faster by raising the temperature of the water.
Fridges and freezers slow down the changes that spoil food.
Catalytic converters in petrol cars change harmful exhaust gases into safer ones.
Washing powders with enzymes break down food stains in cool water.
Paint, oil and galvanising (a coat of zinc) slow the rusting of iron.
Slow-release medicines are coated so that they dissolve over hours.
Factories use an iron catalyst to make ammonia for fertiliser from nitrogen and hydrogen.
Mills and grain stores control dust, because fine dust burns almost all at once.
Pickles use salt, oil and chilli to slow spoiling.
Chemists stir, heat or powder their materials to make a lab reaction finish in time.

open_questions.q: How exactly do enzymes make reactions up to about a thousand billion billion times faster?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can describe how enzymes hold particles in place, but they still argue about every part of the story. Some think quantum tunnelling of hydrogen has a role in some enzymes.

open_questions.q: How did the very first catalysts on Earth begin?
open_questions.why_open: Before there were living cells, something had to speed up chemistry. Some think rocks, metals or small molecules did it. Nobody has shown which came first.

open_questions.q: Could we design catalysts as good as enzymes for any reaction we want?
open_questions.why_open: Chemists have won prizes for making catalysts and for evolving enzymes in the lab. But for many important reactions, we still have no good catalyst.

open_questions.q: Why does the Delhi Iron Pillar's skin form the way it does, and can we copy it?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found out a lot about the skin, but making new iron that protects itself as well and for as long is still hard.

open_questions.q: Can a single reaction be filmed as it happens?
open_questions.why_open: Using very fast flashes of light, scientists have filmed bonds breaking and forming, but only for a few simple reactions so far.

open_questions.q: Are there reactions in space that take longer than the age of the universe?
open_questions.why_open: Some changes, such as the slow decay of certain particles, may be that slow. Scientists are still searching for them, and may never see one finish.

When you stir sugar into tea, what do you think the spoon does?
Why does Amma soak the dal or chana before she cooks it?
What would happen to a pickle if we left out the salt and the oil?
If you wanted a cut apple to stay pale in your tiffin, what would you try?
Which things at home do you think are changing too slowly to see?
Why is a bottle of hydrogen peroxide dark brown?
Where in our house do you see a helper that is not used up?
If you were a particle in a hot cup of tea, what would your day be like?

jokes.a: Because it wanted to meet more people.

jokes.j: What did the catalyst say to the slow reaction?
jokes.a: I will help you out, but do not expect me to change.

jokes.j: Why was the nail so tired?
jokes.a: It had been rusting all week.

jokes.j: What is a cut apple's favourite game?
Why did the pressure cooker get a gold star?

jokes.j: How does the fridge keep the milk calm?

maths.problem: In the Three Cups test, Meenakshi, a girl in Madurai, finds the warm glass fizzes for 14 seconds and the cold glass for 56 seconds. How many times faster is the warm glass?
maths.explain: 56 divided by 14 is 4. The warm glass is 4 times faster. A fair comparison divides the times, because we want to know how many times, not how many seconds apart.
maths.context: In the Three Cups test you time fruit salt in water at different temperatures.
maths.why_maths: Dividing two times tells you how many times faster one reaction is than another, which is clearer than just saying one is quicker.

maths.problem: Many reactions go about twice as fast for each 10 degrees of warmth. A reaction takes 40 minutes at 20 degrees. How long should it take at 30 degrees, at 40 degrees and at 50 degrees?
maths.explain: Each 10 degrees halves the time. Half of 40 is 20. Half of 20 is 10. Half of 10 is 5. This is a rule of thumb and not an exact law, but it is a good guess for many reactions.
maths.context: The Three Cups test shows that warmth speeds up fizz. Chemists have noticed a pattern in how much.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the halving pattern lets you predict a result you have not measured yet.

maths.problem: A jaggery cube has sides of 2 centimetres. Each face is 4 square centimetres, and a cube has 6 faces. Cut into 8 small cubes with sides of 1 centimetre, each small cube has a surface area of 6 square centimetres. By how many square centimetres does the total surface grow?
maths.explain: The big cube has 6 times 4, which is 24 square centimetres. The 8 small cubes have 8 times 6, which is 48. The surface grows by 48 minus 24, which is 24. The same jaggery now has double the surface.
maths.context: In the Apple Race, grated apple browned faster than a chunk because it had more surface.
maths.why_maths: Finding the surface area shows exactly how much more of a solid can meet the air when it is cut small.

maths.problem: In the Apple Race, a plain chunk scores 1 at 10 minutes, 2 at 20 minutes and 4 at 30 minutes. The chunk in lime juice scores 0, 0 and 1. Between which two times did the plain chunk change the most?
maths.answer: Between 20 and 30 minutes, when it rose by 2.
maths.explain: From 10 to 20 minutes it rose from 1 to 2, which is 1. From 20 to 30 minutes it rose from 2 to 4, which is 2. The line is steepest between 20 and 30 minutes.
maths.context: In the Apple Race you score each plate's colour and draw a line graph.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows when a change speeds up or slows down, by how steep the line is.

maths.problem: Lakshmi, a girl in Mysuru, hears that dal takes 45 minutes in an open pot but 15 minutes in a pressure cooker. She puts dal on at 6:10 in each. When does each one finish? How many times faster is the cooker?
maths.answer: The open pot finishes at 6:55, and the cooker at 6:25. The cooker is 3 times faster.
maths.explain: 6:10 plus 45 minutes is 6:55. 6:10 plus 15 minutes is 6:25. 45 divided by 15 is 3, so the cooker is 3 times faster.
maths.context: In Kitchen Clock you ask the cook how long different foods take to cook.
maths.why_maths: Adding minutes to a clock time and dividing two durations are both ways of using a time as a measurement of speed.

maths.problem: In the Same Lime test, each cup has 2 teaspoons of lime juice. Cup A has no water, cup B has 4 teaspoons of water and cup C has 12 teaspoons of water. What fraction of each cup is lime juice?
maths.answer: A is 2 out of 2, which is the whole. B is 2 out of 6, which is one third. C is 2 out of 14, which is one seventh.
maths.explain: The total liquid is 2, 6 and 14 teaspoons. Lime juice is always 2 teaspoons. The fractions are 2/2, 2/6 and 2/14, which simplify to 1, one third and one seventh. The smaller the fraction, the less crowded the acid.
maths.context: In the Same Lime test you add different amounts of water to the same amount of lime juice.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells exactly how crowded the lime juice is, so you can compare cups by number instead of by guess.

maths.problem: The Delhi Iron Pillar is about 1,600 years old. A railway engineer paints an iron bridge every 5 years to stop rust. How many times would the bridge be painted in 1,600 years?
maths.explain: 1,600 divided by 5 is 320. Painting is a barrier that has to be renewed. The pillar's skin has done the same job without anyone repainting it.
maths.context: The Delhi Iron Pillar has rusted very little in about 1,600 years, while painted iron needs new paint every few years.
maths.why_maths: A big number like 1,600 years becomes easier to picture when you compare it with something familiar, like painting every 5 years.

maths.problem: In Meeting Party, four particles in the big square make 6 meetings in 20 seconds. In the small square, the same four make 18 meetings. The small square is a quarter of the area of the big one. How many times more meetings are there in the small square?
maths.explain: 18 divided by 6 is 3. The same particles in a quarter of the space meet 3 times as often. In a real reaction, a bigger crowd in a smaller space also speeds the reaction up. The numbers are a made-up example.
maths.context: In Meeting Party you count handshakes in a big and a small square, to see how crowding changes meetings.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two counts shows how strongly crowding changes the number of meetings.

warmup.a: No. It comes out the same.

Why does a pressure cooker cook dal faster?

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1790s, most chemists thought a metal needed only air or a hot flame to change. Water was just a bystander. A Scottish chemist, Elizabeth Fulhame, tested this. She was soaking cloth in solutions of gold and silver and watching the metals appear as the cloth was exposed to hydrogen and other chemicals. When the cloth was bone dry, nothing happened. When it was damp, the metal appeared. She decided that water took part, but did not seem to be used up. In her view it was made again at the end, ready to work once more. She published all this in a book in 1794. Forty years later, the Swedish chemist Jons Jacob Berzelius gave this kind of helper a name, catalysis. Fulhame's book was read in Britain and America, but she was rarely given credit for the idea of catalysis until chemists looked again at her work in the 1990s.
how_we_found_out.who: Elizabeth Fulhame, a Scottish chemist, and later Jons Jacob Berzelius
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most chemists believed that water was just a bystander in such changes. Fulhame showed that dry cloth did not react at all and damp cloth did, so water was taking part, and coming out ready to work again.

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet cooked or tested at home. Three Cups: the fizz times with half a teaspoon of fruit salt in 150 millilitres are expected to differ clearly (warm shortest, cold longest), but the exact seconds depend on the brand and the room, so the steps ask families to compare the order and repeat each cup twice. Apple Race: a Shimla apple usually browns visibly in 10 to 20 minutes, a slow apple may need up to an hour, and the fridge plate may differ only a little at 30 minutes. Same Lime: foam is small, so compare the time until the fizz stops, and if all three finish together that is written up as a result. Rust Race: salty water usually shows orange rust within a day and plain water in two or three days, and a nail with a chipped coat may rust from the chip. The ideas to check before release: the Delhi Iron Pillar facts (age about 1,600 years, protective skin found at IIT Kanpur), Elizabeth Fulhame's 1794 work and what chemists then believed, the fertiliser figure (now written as four to five in ten people, after Smil and Erisman), the 78 million years enzyme figure (checked, Radzicka and Wolfenden 1995), and the converters claim (now only petrol cars; CNG autos not confirmed). Checked against sources: the pillar's age, location and skin (Wikipedia citing Balasubramaniam), Fulhame 1794 and Berzelius 1835, Zanotto's glass result, and about nine billion years for a proton in the Sun.
